Instrument Battery Test (INSB) is a paper pencil test and 
other two are machine tests. The Instruments Battery Test 
(INSB) comprises two parts. This test assesses assimilation 
of the briefing and the ability of an individual to read and 
interpret the dials of an instrument panel of an aircraft. 
The candidates who score the minimum laid down criteria 
are subjected to the machine test. The machine test 
includes Sensory Motor Apparatus Test (SMA) and 
Control Velocity Test (CVT). These tests measure the 
psychomotor co-ordination skill of the individual. These 
tests are conducted on a single day and administered 
only once in life time.

aimed at assessing a candidate's aptitude to be trained as 
a pilot. PABT is being used as an independent selection 
device to induct potential officers into Flying Branch of

Instrument Battery Test (INSB), Sensory Motor Apparatus 
Test (SMA) and Control Velocity Test (CVT).

Some people believe that they are
masters of their own fate. Other people
see themselves as pawns of fats,
believing that what happens to them in
their lives is due to luck or chance.
The first type, those who believe that
they control their destinies, have been
labelled internals, whereas the latter,
who see their lives as being controlled by
outside forces, have been called
externals.
Internals search more actively for
information before making a decision,
are more motivated to achieve, and
make a greater attempt to control their
environment. Externals, however, are
more compliant and willing to follow
directions. Therefore, internals do well
on sophisticated tasks which include
most, managerial and professional jobs
that require complex information
processing and learning.
In addition, internals are more suited to
jobs that require initiative and
independence of action. Almost all
successful sales people, for instance are
internals. In contrast, externals should
do well on jobs that are well structured
and routine and in which success
depends heavily on complying with the
directions of others.

In AFCAT, every year 4 to 5 questions are asked.
Questions asked from various topics viz., Ancient History (Harappan
Sites, Vedic Age, Maurayan, Nanda and Pallava Dynasty); Medieval
History (Delhi Sultanate, Mughal Empire and Battles); Modern
History (Governor-Generals and National Movements).
ANCIENT INDIA
Indus Valley Civilisation
(2500 BC – 1750 BC)
Indus valley civilisation is one of the earliest civilisations
of the world and it was an urban civilisation.
Harappan civilisation was named by John Marshall after
the first discovered Harappa site in 1921 by Dayaram
Sahni.
In this civilisation, people were familiar with gold, silver,
bronze, lead and copper, but iron was not known to them.
Important features of this civilisation are systematic town
planning, used burnt bricks to construct houses, well
managed drainage system, Great Bath and Granaries
(Mohenjodaro).
Indus people first produced cotton which the Greeks
termed as Sindon. They mainly produced wheat, barley,
rai, peas, seausum, rice and mustard.
Harappans looked on Earth as fertility Goddess and,
phallic (lingum) and yoni worship was prevalent.
Unicorn and pipal tree also were worshipped.
This civilisation belongs to Bronze Age.

Lumbini (Nepal) in year 563 BC. His birth is symbolised

His father was Suddhodana (king of Kapilavastu) and

He was married at the age of 16 to Yashodhara and had a
son Rahul.
He renounced (left) his home at the age of 29. This is known
as Mahabhinishkramana. (Symbol : Horse)
At Bodhgaya, under the Bodhi tree, he attained Nirvana,
on the bank of river Niranjana (modern name Falgu).
(Symbol : Bodhi Tree)
He delivered his first sermon at Sarnath. This is known as
Dharmachakrapravartana. (Symbol : Wheel)

He founded Jain Sangha (Jain Commune) at Pava.
He died in 527 BC, at the age of 72 in Pavapuri.
After attaining the Kaivalya, he is called as Jinas,
Nirgranthas.

General Awareness
Magadha Empire
Magadha was one of the most powerful mahajanapadas. It
was ruled by many dynasties such as Haryanka dynasty,
Shishunaga dynasty, Nanda dynasty, Maurya dynasty and
Guptas.
Bimbisara (554-492 BC) was the first ruler of Magadha
empire. He was the founder of Haryanka dynasty and
built the city of Rajagriha.
Ajatashatru (492-460 BC) was the son of Bimbisara and
occupied the throne by killing his father.
Udayin (460-444 BC) son of Ajatashatru, founded the city
of Pataliputra and shifted the capital of Magadha from
Rajagriha to Pataliputra.
The last Nanda king Dhanananda ruled Magadha during
the Alexander’s invasion of India (326 BC).
The Nanda dynasty came to an end in
322-21 BC and was replaced by Mauryan Empire.
Alexander’s Invasion (326 BC)
Alexander of Macedonia fought the ‘Battle of
Vitasta’ or ‘Battle of Hydaspes’ with Porus (ruler
of India) to conquer Indian territory.
This battle was fought on the bank of river Jhelum.
He failed to conquer India and died in 323 BC at Babylon.
Mauryan Empire (322–185 BC)
Chandragupta Maurya, assisted by Chanakya overthrew
Dhanananda to lay the foundation of Maurayan dynasty.
He defeated Seleucus Nicator. Megasthenese, the Greek
Ambassador of Seleucus, visited the court of
Chandragupta Maurya.
During his region Megasthenese wrote Indica and
Kautilya (Vishnugupta, Chanakya) wrote Arthashastra.
Bindusara son and successor of Chandragupta Maurya
was famous as Amitroghata.
Ashoka was a great ruler, he succeeded Bindusara. He
fought Kalinga war in 261 BC.
It was the last war fought by Ashoka.
His Rock Edict XIII talked about Kalinga war. Mostly
used Prakrit language in his inscriptions. These
inscriptions are first deciphered by James Princep in 1837.
Ashoka is also called Devanampriya and Piyadasi.
Sanchi stupa was built by Ashoka.
Brihadratha was the last Mauryan ruler.
Post-Mauryan Dynasties
The Indo-Greeks
The most famous Indo Greek ruler was Menander
(165-145 BC), also known as Milinda.
Greeks were the first to issue coins which are attributed to
the kings and also the first to issue gold coins in India.
Nagasen, a Bodh Bhikshu composed Milind Panho which
was in Question-Answer form between Nagasen and
Menander.
The Shakas or Scythians
The Greeks were followed by the Shakas, who controlled
a larger part of India than the Greek did.
Vikramaditya defeated Shakas in 58 BC, on this occasion
he started Vikram era.
The Parthians
The most famous Parthian King was Gondophernes (AD
19-45). During his period, in AD 1st century, Ist Christian
missionary under St Thomas visited India.
The Kushanas (AD 45)
Kushanas came from North Central Asia near China.
Their empire included a good part of Central Asia, a portion
of Iran, a portion of Afghanistan, Pakistan and almost the
whole of North India.
Kushanas were the first ruler to issue gold coins on large
scale.
Kanishka was most famous king.
He patronised the following persons
Ashwaghosha (wrote ‘Buddhacharita’)
Nagarjuna
Vasumitra (Chairman of fourth Buddhist Council)
Charak (a physician, wrote ‘Charak Samhita’)
He started an era in AD 78, which is now known as Saka
era and is used by the Government of India.
The Gupta Age (AD 319-AD 540)
Sri Gupta was the founder of this dynasty who was
succeeded by Ghatotkacha.
Chandra Gupta-I was first Gupta ruler to assume the title
of Maharajadhiraj.He started Gupta Era  in AD 319-20.
Samudragupta is also called ‘Napoleon of India’ by VA
Smith. His court poet Harisena composed Prayag Prashasti
(Allahabad Pillar Inscription).
Chandragupta-II (Vikramaditya), Mehrauli Iron Pillar
(Near Qutub Minar, Delhi) is dedicated to him. The
famous poet Kalidasa (also known Shakespeare of India)
lived in his court. Fa-hien, a chinese pilgrim, visited his
court.
Kumaragupta-I founded Nalanda university.
Skandagupta repaired Sudarshan lake. Gupta empire
was attacked by Huns during his reign.
The official language of gupta period was Sanskrit.

MEDIEVAL INDIA
Muslim Invasions in India
Mohammad Bin Qasim was the first Muslim invader. He
invaded India in AD 712.
Mahmud Ghaznavi was the first Turkish invader. He
invaded India in AD 998. He led 17 expeditions to India
and destroyed Somnath temple in AD 1025.
Mohammad Ghori was defeated by Prithviraj Chauhan
III in first Battle of Tarain (1191).
He defeated him in second Battle of Tarain (1192). After
his death, his slave Qutubuddin Aibak established Delhi
Sultanate.
Delhi Sultanate
Slave Dynasty (AD 1206-90)
Qutubuddin Aibak founded Slave dynasty. He started
the construction of Qutub Minar (Delhi) and built
Adhai-din ka Jhopra mosque in Ajmer. He died while
playing Chaugan or Polo in 1206 at Lahore.
Iltutmish was the slave of Aibak. He introduced silver
coin (tanka) and copper coin (jittal) and completed the
construction of Qutub Minar. He made Delhi the capital
in place of Lahore.
Razia Sultan was the daughter of Iltutmish and the first
woman emperor of India.
Ghiyasuddin Balban took the title of Zil-i-Ilahi. He
introduced Sijda and Paibos (forms of salutation) and
established military department Diwan-i-Arz.
Kaiqubad was the last ruler of Slave dynasty.
Khilji Dynasty (AD 1290-1320)
Jalaluddin Khilji was the founder of Khilji dynasty.
Alauddin Khilji was the first Sultan of Delhi who
separated religion from politics. He introduced Dagh
(branding of horse) and Chehra (descriptive role of
soldiers). He also introduced market reforms. He built
Alai Darwaja (Delhi). He also abolished Iqta system.
Malik Kafur was the chief of Military under Alauddin
Khilji and was given the title ‘Hazar Dinari’.

Chinese pilgrim, Hieun Tsang visited the court during his

His capital was Kannauj.
Banabhatta, who adorned his court wrote Harshacharita and

The Satavahanas
This dynasty was founded by Simuka (60-37 BC).
Land grant system to Brahmins was started by Satavahanas.
The official language of the Satavahanas was Prakrit.
Gautamiputra Satakarni was a famous king of this dynasty.
Rashtrakutas
This dynasty was founded by Dantidurga.
Their king, Krishna I constructed famous rock-cut
Kailasha temple at Ellora.
The Chalukyas
Chalukyas of Vatapi (Badami) was founded by
Pulakeshin I.
Pulakeshin II (611-642) was contemporary of Harsha.
The Pallavas
This dynasty was founded by Simha Vishnu.
Narsimhavarman was their greatest king. He founded
the town of Mamalapuram (Mahabalipuram) which he
adorned with beautiful rock-cut Raths or Seven Pagoras.
The Cholas
This dynasty was founded by Vijayalaya and its
capital was Tanjore.
The greatest Chola rulers were Rajaraja I (985-1014)
and his son Rajendra I (1014-1044).
Dancing figure of Shiva called Nataraja belongs to this
period only.
The Palas of Bengal
Its founder was Gopala (AD 750).
He was Patron of Buddhism. Dharampala founded
Vikramsila University and revived Nalanda
University.

Tughlaq Dynasty (AD 1320-1414)
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq was the founder of the Tughlaq
dynasty.
Mohammad Bin Tughlaq transferred capital from Delhi
to Devagiri (later named Daulatabad). He also introduced
token currency and established Diwan-i-Kohi
(Department of Agriculture).
Firoz Shah Tughlaq made Jaziya as a separate tax. He also
imposed water tax (Hasil-i-Sharb). He built many canals and
established a hospital (Dar-ul-Shifa) at Delhi.
Timur, the lame, was a Turkish chief. He invaded India in
AD 1398 during the reign of Muhammad Shah Tughlaq.
Sayyid Dynasty (AD 1414-50). It was founded by Khizr
Khan.
Khizr Khan took the title Rayat-i-Ala and not a king.
Lodhi Dynasty (AD 1451-1526)
Bahlol Lodhi founded Lodhi dynasty. It was the first
Afghan dynasty.
Sikandar Lodhi introduced Gaz-i-Sikandari. He also
shifted his capital from Delhi to Agra.
Ibrahim Lodhi was the last king of Lodhi dynasty and
also last Sultan of Delhi.
Mughal Dynasty
Babur laid the foundation of Mughal empire in India in
AD 1526. His autobiography is Tuzuk-i-Baburi. He died at
Agra and his tomb is at Kabul.
Humayun was the son of Babur, he built Din Panah at Delhi
as his second capital. His biography ‘Humayunama’ was
written by his sister Gulbadan Begum. He was burried in
Delhi after his death in AD 1556. His Tomb (Delhi) built by
his wife Haji Begum.
Sher Shah Suri (1540-45)
¢ Sher Shah Suri was the founder of Sur dynasty.
¢ He issued coin called Rupia.
¢ He built the Grand Trunk Road (G.T. Road)
Akbar ascended the throne under the title of Jalaluddin
Muhammad Akbar Badshah Ghazi. He founded Fatehpur
Sikri and proclaimed a new religion called, Din-i-Ilahi, and
Birbal was the only hindu who joined it. He abolished
Jaziya and built Agra Fort, Lahore Fort, Buland Darwaja,
Allahabad Fort. His court had nine jewels (navaratnas). He
was  buried at Sikandra near Agra.
Jahangir son of Akbar, established Zanzir-i-Adal (chain of
justice). He wrote his memoirs Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri. He was
buried in Lahore.
Shah Jahan was the son of Jagat Gosai and Jahangir. He
built Moti Masjid (Agra), Taj Mahal (Agra), Jama Masjid
(Delhi). He was buried at Taj Mahal (Agra).
Aurangzeb adopted the title of Alamgir. He executed
Guru Tegh Bahadur (9th Sikh Guru). He built Moti Masjid
(in Red Fort, Delhi). He was called Zinda Pir and was
buried at Daulatabad.

Assumed the title Shah Alam I also known as
Shah-i-Bekhabar.

He became king with the help of Julfiqar Khan (Persian

Farukhsiyar
He ascended the throne with the help of Sayyid Brothers.
Mohammad Shah
He was pleasure loving king and was nick named ‘Rangeela’.
Shah Alam II
Shah Alam joined hands with Mir Qasim of Bengal and
Shiraj-ud-Daulah of Awadh in the Battle of Buxar
against British in 1764.
He defeated Maratha in 3rd Battle of Panipat.
Bahadur Shah Zafar
Bahadur Shah Zafar was the last Mughal emperor. He
was the leader of Revolt of 1857.

Revolt of 1857

place in different parts of the country. It is considered as
the first war of Indian independence.

They moved to Delhi, where Bahadur Shah Zafar (the last
Mughal emperor) was declared as the leader of the revolt.
He was given the title of ‘Shahenshahi-e-Hindustan’.

Indian National Movement
Indian National Congress
Indian National Congress (INC) was formed in 1885 by
AO Hume.
First session was held at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit
college, Bombay  and presided over by WC Banerjee.
Swadeshi and Boycott Movement
Partition of Bengal came into effect on 16th
October, 1905. It was announced by Lord Curzon.
The Congress leaders and nationalists of Bengal firmly
opposed the partition of Bengal.
INC took Swadeshi call in 1905 at Benaras session.
Lala Lajpat Rai took the movement to Punjab. There was
boycott of foreign goods and picketing of shops selling
liquor.
Rabindranath Tagore composed ‘Amar Sonar Bangla’ song.
Muslim League and Surat Split
Muslim League was established in 1906 by Nawab
Salimullah at Dhaka (then Dacca). In Surat session (1907),
Congress splits got divided into two wings: Moderates
and Extremists.
Moderates were led by Gopal Krishna Gokhale.
Extremists were led by Lala Lajpat Rai (Lal), Bal
Gangadhar Tilak (Bal) and Bipin Chandra Pal (Pal). Bal
Gangadhar Tilak is also known as father of Indian unrest
and father of revolutionary ideas.
Morley-Minto Reforms (1909)
The reforms envisaged a separate electorate for Muslims,
besides other constitutional measures.
Lord Minto came to be known as the father of communal
electorate.

Home Rule Movement
It was started by Tilak on 28th April, 1916 and Annie Besant
in September, 1916. The main objective of this movement
was ‘Swaraj’.
Gandhi’s Arrival in India
In 1915, Gandhiji arrived in Bombay from South Africa.
In 1916, he founded Sabarmati Ashram on the banks of river
Sabarmati in Gujarat. He led the three major struggles.
Champaran Satyagrah was the first Civil Disobedience
Movement in India by Gandhiji. He redressed the grievances
of the Indigo cultivators of Champaran (Bihar) and fought
against teen-kathia system.
Ahmedabad Satyagraha Mahatma Gandhi supported the
workers against mill owners, as workers demanded increase
in wages. It was Gandhiji’s first hunger strike and resulted
in increase in wages.
Kheda Satyagraha He supported the cause of peasants for
remission of revenue demand, due to crop failure. It was
first Non-cooperation movement led by Gandhiji.
Rowlatt Act 1919
In 1919, a sedition committee headed by Justice Rowlatt led
to the Rowlatt Act.
This act gave unbridled powers to the government to arrest
and imprison suspects without trial hence deemed as Black
Act.
Jallianwala Bagh Massacre
The massacre took place on 13th April 1919, in Jallianwala
Bagh, at Amritsar (Punjab) where people gathered to protest
against the arrest of Dr. Satyapal and Dr Kitchlu the occasion
was the Baisakhi celebration.
General Dyer opened fire on the peaceful protesters. Sardar
Udham Singh murdered General Dyer in London in 1940.
Non-cooperation Movement
INC at its Calcutta Session (1920) passed Non- cooperation
resolution.
Non-cooperation movement launched by Gandhiji in August
1920. There was boycott of schools, colleges, courts, surrender
of titles etc.
Local police station was put on fire by a group of angry
peasants known as Chauri-Chaura Incident (1922).
Gandhiji called off the non-cooperation movement after this.
Swaraj Party and Kakori Conspiracy
Swaraj Party founded by Motilal Nehru, CR Das and NC
Kelkar in 1923.
A train robbery was took place at Kakori station on 9th
August, 1925.
The robbery conspiracy was executed by Ram Prasad Bismil,
Ashfaqula Khan and others of Hindustan Republican
Association (HRA).
Simon Commission
It was constituted by John Simon to review the political
situation in India and suggest constitutional reforms.
Indian leaders opposed the commission as all the
members were white and passed resolution in Madras
session of INC under MA Ansari to boycott this.
Lahore Session (1929)
In this session, Jawaharlal Nehru became the President
of INC and Poorna Swaraj was declared as ultimate
goal of INC.
26th January, 1930 was adopted as the first
independence day and tri-colour flag was unfurled on
the banks of river Ravi in Lahore.
Dandi March (1930)
It was also called the Salt Satyagraha.
Gandhiji started march from Sabarmati Ashram to
Dandi on 12th March, 1930 with 78 followers.
Gandhi ji broke the salt law at Dandi on 5th April, 1930.
Round Table Conference
First Round Table Conference (1930) held in London
between the British and Indians to discuss Simon
Commission report, but failed due to the absence of
INC.
Second Round Table Conference (1931) held in
London during Viceroyalty of Lord Willingdon.
Gandhiji attended it on behalf of Indian National
Congress.
Third Round Table Conference (1932) This conference
failed in achieving its target because all national
leaders were in jail.
Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)
It was signed between Lord Irwin and Gandhiji
(representing INC).
In this pact, INC agreed to call off Civil Disobedience
Movement and join the Second Round Table
Conference.
Poona Pact (1932)
It was signed between Gandhiji and BR Ambedkar.
In this joint electorate was accepted, but seats reserved
for depressed class in provincial legislature were
increased.
Government of India Act, 1935
Act provided for the establishment of an All India
federation and a new system of government for
provinces on the basis of provincial autonomy.
Act provided for a federal court and a federal bank.
10

Cripps Mission (1942)
This Mission was sent to get Indian cooperation in World
War II.
It was headed by Stafford Cripps and offered ‘Dominion
Status’ for India.
Quit India Movement (1942)
INC passed the Quit India Resolution at Gwoliya Tank,
Bombay. In this movement Gandhiji gave the slogan of ‘Do
or Die’.
Parallel governments were established like : Balia (UP)
led by Chittu Pandey, Tamluk (Bengal) led by Satish
Samanta, Satara (Maharashtra) led by YB Chavan and
Talcher (Odisha).
The slogan of ‘Quit India’ was given by Yusuf Meher Ali.
Indian National Army
INA was founded by General Mohan Singh in 1942.
In 1943, Rashbehari Bose handed over the leadership of
INA to Subhash Chandra Bose.Subhash Chandra Bose
set-up Indian League at Berlin around 1941.
Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)
Members in Cabinet mission were Lord Pethick
Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and AV Alexander. It provided
that the Constituent Assembly would be elected by the
members of Provincial Legislative Assembly.
This was followed by ‘Direct Action Day’ on 16th August,
1946.
Attlee’s Announcement and
Mountbatten Plan
British PM Attlee announced that the British would
withdraw from India by 30th June, 1948.
The Mountbatten plan was announced on 3rd June, 1947
which decided that India to be divided into two
independent dominions of India and Pakistan.
Indian Independence Act (1947)
It abolished the sovereignty of British Parliament and
established dominions of India and Pakistan. Lord
Mountbatten became first Governor-General of free
India.
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel integrated all princely states by
15th August, 1947 except Kashmir, Junagarh and
Hyderabad.
The Annexation of Hyderabad and
Liberation of Goa
Princely State of Hyderabad merged into Union of India
after operation polo in November, 1949.
Armed action carried out by the Indian armed forces
incorporated Goa into Union of India.

In AFCAT, every year 2 to 3 questions are asked. Topics from which
questions were mainly asked are World Geography (Latitude,
Eclipse, Continents, Atmospheric Layers);
Indian Geography (Mountain, Rivers, Soils, Crop Production);
Ecology and Environment (Pollution, National park) etc.
WORLD GEOGRAPHY
Universe
The study of universe is known as Cosmology.
The universe is commonly defined as the totality of
everything that exists including all physical matter and
energy, the planets, stars, galaxies and the contents of
intergalactic space.
A galaxy is a vast system of billions of stars, dust and gases
bound by their own gravity.
There are 100 billion galaxies in the universe and each
galaxy has on average 100 billion stars.
Our galaxy is Milky Way Galaxy (or the Akash Ganga)
formed after the Big Bang.
Stars are the heavenly bodies made up of hot burning
gases and they shine by emitting their own light.
Satellites are the heavenly bodies that revolve around the
planets. Moon is the natural satellite of the Earth.
Solar System
The solar system consists of the Sun, the eight planets and
their satellites (or Moons) and thousands of other smaller
heavenly bodies such as asteroids, comets and meteors.
The Sun is at the centre of the solar system and all these
bodies revolve around it. It is the nearest star to the Earth.
Eight planets according to their distance from the Sun are
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus
and Neptune.
The ninth planet ‘Pluto’ has been removed from the
family of the solar system in 2006.
Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are called  the terrestrial
planets because their structure is similar to that of the
Earth.
In Solar System, four Jovian planets exist, these are
-Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. These are gas gaint
so designated as ‘Jovian’.

Rocks
The solid part of the Earth’s crust is called ‘Rock.’
Rocks are made up of two or more minerals.
Rocks are classified into three main types
(i) Igneous Rocks (Granite, Basalt, Gabbro)
(ii) Sedimentary Rocks (Sandstone, Gypsum, Limestone,
Dolomite)
(iii) Metamorphic Rocks (Marble, Quartzite, Gneiss, Slate)
Volcano
A volcano is a vent or opening through which Lava comes
out. Types of volcanoes on the basis of periodicity of eruption
(i) Active Volcano A volcano is said to be active if it
shows signs of unrest and have erupted in recent
past. e.g. Mount Etna, Mount Stromboli etc.
(ii) Dormant Volcano A volcano which has not erupted
in near past but it is capable of erupting in future. e.g.
Fujiyama.
(iii) Extinct Volcano A volcano which shows no signs of
eruption in future. e.g. Hawaiian Emperor, Kohala
etc.
Earthquakes
Earthquake is simply shaking of the ground caused by
movement of the Earth’s crust.
Focus is the point beneath the Earth where earthquake
originates.
Epicentre is the point just above the focus on the Earth’s
surface.
The magnitude of earthquake is measured by Richter
scale.
The intensity of earthquake is measured by Mercalli scale.
Tsunami
Tsunami is large ocean wave that is caused by sudden
motion on the ocean floor. Motion could be an earthquake,
volcanic eruption or underwater landslide.

Climate
Climate refers to the sum total of the atmospheric
conditions in terms of temperature, pressure, wind,
moisture, cloudiness, precipitation and visibility of a
particular place at any given time.
India has tropical monsoon type of climate.
Factors affecting Indian climate are
_ Locational and latitudinal extent
_ Distance from sea
_ The Northern mountain range
_ Physiography
_ Monsoon winds
Mawsynram a village in Meghalaya receiver highest
rainfall in India.
Seasons in India
A season is a division of the year marked by changes in
weather, temperature and amount of daylight.
Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) has recognised
four seasons
(i) Winter Season (November to March)
(ii) Summer Season (March to June)
(iii) Rainy Season or Advancing Monsoon (June to
September)
(iv) Retreating Monsoon (Mid September to November)
Rain in India is mainly brought by South-West monsoon
in summer.
In winter season, the North-Western part of India gets
rainfall from Western cyclonic disturbances and Southern
Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu gets rainfall from
retreating monsoon or North-East trade winds.

Agriculture
Agriculture is the primary source of livelihood for about 58% of India’s population.
There are three crop seasons in India
(i) Kharif sown in June/July and harvested in September/October e.g. Rice, jowar, bajra, ragi, maize, cotton and jute.
(ii) Rabi sown in October/December and harvested in April/May. e.g. Wheat, barley, peas, rapeseed and mustard.
(iii) Zaid grown for two months i.e. April/June. e.g. Melon, watermelon, cucumber and vegetables.

The most important means of transport in India are

Roadways
It mainly consists of National Highways, State Highways
and other district and rural roads.
The longest National Highway in India is NH44. It connects
Srinagar to Kanyakumari.

fourth largest in the world.

elephant.

km.

1925 between Victoria Terminus and Kurla.

_ Broad Gauge (Distance between rails is 1.676 m)
_ Metre Gauge (Distance between rails is 1.00 m)
_ Narrow Gauge (Distance between rails is 0.762 or 0.610
m)
The longest railway platform in India is Gorakhpur with a

Vivek Express has the longest train route in India. It
connects Dibrugarh and Kanyakumari.

Maharaja Express.

India that runs between Delhi and Jhansi.
The Darjeeling Himalayan railway is given the nickname

India’s first fully made in India train. It is fastest train of

Environment and Ecology
Environment includes all external conditions, factors, matter
and energy of living and non-living that affect any living
organism or other specified system.
Ecology is a science, in which study of organism is
undertaken in relation to their environment. The term
ecology was coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1869.
Ecosystem is a set of biotic (Living beings) and abiotic
(Non-living beings) components connected by the
exchange of matter and energy.
The main function of an ecosystem includes transfer of
energy and nutrients into environment mainly through
Food web and Food chain.
Food Chain is the flow of energy from one organisms to
another in a sequence of food transfer.
Food Web is a network of food chain by which energy and
nutrients are passed from one species of living organism
to another.
Biome refers to terrestrial regions characterised by certain
types of vegetation and other forms of life. Example
includes various types of deserts, grasslands and forests.
Ozone (O3) It is colourless and highly reactive gas and a
major component of photochemical smog. It is found in
the ozone layer in the stratosphere and protect us from
ultra violet rays. The stratospheric ozone is depleting due
to increasing concentration of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)
in the atmosphere.
Acid Rain It is a form of precipitation that is usually
acidic, meaning that it has elevated levels of hydrogen
ions (low pH). Acid rain is caused by emissions of sulfur
dioxide and nitrogen oxide. It can have harmful effects on
plants, aquatic animals and infrastructure.
Artificial Rain refers to artificially inducing moisture in
the clouds to cause rainfall. It is produced by seeding
clouds with silver iodide or dry ice using an aircraft or an
artillery gun.
Environmental pollution is the effect of undesirable
changes in our surroundings that has harmful effects on
plants, animals and human beings.
Primary Pollutant is the one which directly enters into
environment e.g. So ,
2 CFC, CO2 etc.
Secondary Pollutant does not enter directly into
environment but form when one pollutant react with
other pollutant e.g. O3, Peroxyacetyl Nitrate, etc.
Pollution is mainly divided into Air pollution, Water
pollution, Noise pollution, Land pollution and
Radioactive pollution.

Framing of the Indian Constitution
Idea to have a Constitution was given by MN Roy in 1934.
The demand for the Constituent Assembly was first
accepted by the British in August Offer of 1940.
The Constituent Assembly was set-up in November, 1946
as per the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946.
There were to be total of 389 members in the Constituent
Assembly of which 292 were representatives of the states,
93 represented the princely states and 4 were from the
Chief Commissioner provinces.
At the time of Independence there were 565 princely
states in India.
The first meeting of Constituent Assembly was held on
9th December, 1946 with Dr Sacchidanand Sinha as its
Provisional President. Its last session was held on
24th January, 1950.
Dr Rajendra Prasad and HC Mukherjee were elected as
President and Vice-President respectively on 11th
December, 1946.
Drafting Committee was constituted on 29th August, 1947
with Dr BR Ambedkar as the Chairman.
Other members of Drafting Committee included N
Gopala Swamy Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar,
Dr KM Munshi, Syed Mohammad Saadullah, N Madhava
Rau (replaced BL Mitter) and TT Krishnamachari
(replaced DP Khaitan).
The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and
18 days  to complete the Constitution.
The Constitution was adopted on 26th November, 1949.
On 24th January, 1950 ‘Jana Gana Mana’ adopted as
National Anthem.
The Constitution came into force on 26th January, 1950
because on this, in 1930 Purna Swaraj day was celebrated
by Indian ‘National Congress’ (INC). 26th January is
celebrated as Republic Day in India.
Originally, the Constitution contained 395 Articles, 22
parts and 8 schedules. Presently, it has 448 Articles, 25
Parts and 12 Schedules.

Salient Features of the Constitution
The Indian Constitution is the lengthiest written
Constitution in the world.
Under the Constitution, the people of India are the
ultimate sovereign.
The Indian Constitution stands for a Secular state.
Constitution contains federal features as well as ‘Unitary
features’.
Constitution provides single citizenship to its citizens.
There is a single, integrated and independent judiciary in
India.
Indian Constitution has special provision of emergency.
Article 326 of Constitution of India deals with elections to
the House of the People and to the legislative assemblies
of the states on the basis of adult suffrage.
The procedure of Amendment of the Constitution is
partly flexible and partly rigid.

The Preamble
The Preamble means introduction or preface of the
Constitution or essence of the Constitution. NA Palkhiwala
an eminent jurist and constitutional expert called the
Preamble as the identity card of the Constitution.
The Preamble of the Indian Constitution is based on the
objective resolution drafted and moved by Jawaharlal
Nehru on 13th December, 1946 and adopted by the
Constituent Assembly.
Our Preamble starts with : We, the People of India, having
solemnly resolved to constitute India into a Sovereign,
Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic and to secure to all its
citizens.
Justice Social, Economic and Political.
Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
Equality of status and of opportunity and to promote
among them all.
The words-Socialist, Secular and Integrity were added to
Preamble by 42nd Amendment Act of 1976.
Union and its Territory
Article 1-4 under Part I of the Constitution deals with
the Union and its Territories.
Article 1 describes India, that is Bharat as the Union of
states and the territory of India shall comprise of
– Territories of the states
– Union Territories
– Territories that may be acquired by the Government of India
at any time. (Dadra and Nagar Haveli was acquired from
Portuguese in 1954; Goa, Daman and Diu was annexed from
Portuguese in 1961 and Puducherry was acquired from
French in 1954)
Article 2 empowers the Parliament to admit new states
into the Union of India or establish new states on such
terms and conditions as it thinks fit.
Article 3 authorises the Parliament to form a new state or
alter the areas, boundaries or names of existing states.
After formation of Jammu & Kashmir, there are 28 states
and 8 Union Territories of Indian Union Consists.
Citizenship
Citizenship is the position or status of being a citizen of
a particular country.
Articles 5 to 11 deals with various provisions of
citizenship.
In India, citizenship can be acquired by following ways

2. By Descent (person born outside India, but his/her

Citizenship of a Person in India can be lost due to

3. By Deprivation Due to fraud, false representation
given by a person. The citizenship (Amendment) Act,
2019 amends the citizenship Act, 1955. This
Amendment Act provides that the Hindus, Sikh,
Buddhist, Jains, Parsi and christians from Afghanistan,
Bangladesh, Pakistan who entered India on or before
31 Dec. 2014 will not be treated as illegal migrants
and will be eligible for grant citizenship.

Fundamental Right (Article 12-35)
The Fundamental Rights are provided in Part III of the
Indian Constitution.
Originally, there were seven Fundamental Rights but later
right to property was removed from Fundamental Rights
by 44th Amendment Act, 1948. Therefore, six
Fundamental Rights are given as
1. Rights to Equality (Article 14-18)
Equality before law (Article 14)
Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race,
caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15)
Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment
(Article 16)
Abolition of untouchability (Article 17)
Abolition of titles (Article 18)
2. Rights to Freedom (Article 19-22)
Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech
and expression, assembly, association, movement,
residence and profession (Article 19)
Protection in respect of conviction for offences (Article 20)
Protection of life and personal liberty (Article 21)
Free and compulsory education to all children of the age
6-14 years (Right to Education under Article 21A)
Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases
(Article 22)
3. Rights against Exploitation
(Article 23-24)
Prohibition of human trafficking and forced labour
(Article 23)
Prohibition of employment of children in factories etc
(Article 24)
4. Rights to Freedom of Religion
(Article 25-28)
Freedom of conscience and right to profess, practice and
propagate one’s religious beliefs
Freedom to manage religious affairs (Article 26)
Freedom from taxation for promotion of any particular
religion (Article 27)
Freedom from attendance of religious instructions or
religious worship in certain educational institutions
(Article 28)
5. Cultural and Educational Rights
(Article 29-30)
Protection of language, script and culture of minorities
(Article 29)
Right of minorities to establish and administer
educational institutions (Article 30)
6. Rights to Constitutional Remedies
(Article 32 and Article 226)
Right to move to the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the
High courts (Article 226) in case of violation of the
Fundamental Rights.

Constitution.

Fundamental Duties
Fundamental Duties are the acts which the citizens are
suppose to perform while exercising their rights. It is
covered under Article 51
options:
of the Constitution.
In 1976, the Fundamental Duties of citizen were added by
42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 on the
recommendation of Swaran Singh Committee.
Originally, there were 10 Fundamental Duties but in 2002
by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, eleventh
Fundamental Duty was added.
Union Executive
Part V of the Constitution contains the provision with
respect to the Union Government and Article 52-78 deal
with Union Executive.
The Union Executive consists of the President, the
Vice-President, the Prime Minister with his Council of
Minister and Attorney General of India.
The President
Article 52, provides the office of the President of India.
The President is the head of the state and he is the first
citizen of India.
Any Indian citizen who has completed 35 years of age
and doesn’t hold any office of profit and also qualified for
election as member of Lok Sabha is eligible for election to
the post of President of India.
President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral
college in accordance with the system of proportional
representation by means of single transferable vote
system and secret ballot.
The electoral college consist of elected members of both
the Houses of Parliament, elected members of State
Legislative Assemblies and elected members of
Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry.
All doubts and disputes regarding election of President
are dealt by Supreme Court of India.
According to Article 56(1), the tenure of President is
5 years.
Under Article 61, President can be impeached from office
for violation of the Constitution.
Power and Function of the President
1. Executive Power He appoints Prime Minister, other
Ministers, Chief Justice and judges of Supreme Court
and High Court, the Attorney General of India and
other Executive Heads.
All executive actions of the Government of India are
formally taken in the name of President.
2. Legislative Power Power to summon or prorogue the
Parliament and dissolve the Lok Sabha. He nominates
12 members in Rajya Sabha and 2 members of
Anglo-Indian community in the Lok Sabha.
A bill becomes an act of the Indian Parliament only
after it receives the assent of the President.
3. Financial Power Money Bills are introduced in
Parliament with his prior recommendation. He
ensures that Annual Financial Statement (budget) is
laid before Parliament.
4. Emergency Power
National Emergency (Article 352) can be declared on
grounds of war, external aggression or armed
rebellion.
Constitutional Emergency (Article 356) also known
as President Rule can be proclaimed due to failure of
the constitutional machinery in state.
Financial Emergency (Article 360) can be declared
when financial stability of India is threatened.
5. Veto Power President of India is vested with three Veto
powers i.e. Absolute, Suspensive and Pocket which he
can use to deny the execution of an action
recommended by Parliament.
Types of Veto
(i) Absolute Veto Withholding of assent to the bill
passed by the legislature
(ii) Suspensive Veto Sending back of a bill, which can
be superseded by the legislature with an ordinary
majority.
(iii) Pocket veto Taking no action on the bill passed by
the legislature. It was used in 1986 in case of postal
bill by the then President Giani Zail Singh.
6. Military Power President as supreme commander of
defence forces appoints respective chiefs of Army,
Navy and Air force.
7. Pardoning Power Article 72 of the constitution
empowers the President to grant pardons to persons
who have been tried and convicted of certain
offences.
8. Ordinance Making Power Article 123 of the
constitution empowers the President to promulgate
ordinances during the recess of parliament. These
ordinances have the same force and effect as an act of
parliament, but are temporary in nature.
Vice-President
Article 63 of the Constitution provides for the post of
Vice-President of India.
He holds office for a term of 5 years.
Articles 66(1) provides for his election by an electoral college
consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament.
Any Indian citizen who have completed 35 years of age
and is qualified for election as a member of Rajya Sabha is
eligible for election as Vice-President. Also he should not
hold any office of profit under union or State Government
or under any public authority.

Chairman of Rajya Sabha, he cannot vote in the first instance
but can cast a vote in the case of an equality of votes.
He acts as the President when a vacancy occurs in the office
of the President due to resignation, removal, death or
otherwise.

Council of Ministers
Article 74 and Article 75 deal with the provision
regarding Council of Ministers.
Article 74 states that there shall be a Council of Ministers
with the Prime Minister as the head to advise the President.
The total number of Ministers, including the Prime
Minister, in the Council of Minister shall not exceed 15%
of the total strength of the Lok Sabha. This provision was
inserted in Constitution through 91st Amendment Act,
2003.
Prime Minister
In the Parliamentary system of government, Prime
Minister is the real executive authority.
He is the head of the government and appointed by the
President as per the provisions explained under Article 75
of the Constitution.
The term of the Prime Minister is not fixed as he holds
office during the pleasure of the President.
He presides over the meeting of Council of Ministers and
influences their decisions.
He can ask a minister to resign or advise the President to
dismiss him in case of differences of opinion.
Parliamentary sessions are summoned by the President
on the recommendation of Prime Minister. The maximum
interval between two sessions of a Parliament can be 6
months.

Attorney General of India
Attorney General of India is appointed by the President
under Article 76 of the Constitution.
Term of Attorney General is not fixed by the Constitution,
he holds office during the pleasure of the President.
He appears on behalf of Central Government in all the
cases in the Supreme Court.
He has the right of audience in all courts in the territory of
India and has the right to speak and to take part in the
proceedings of both Houses of Parliament.
The Union Legislature
The Union Legislature also known as Parliament consists
of the President, Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
Article 79-122 in Part V deals with the provisions of the
Parliament.
Rajya Sabha
According to Article 80, Rajya Sabha consists of not more
than 250 members of whom 12 shall be nominated by the
President and the remaining 238 shall be representatives
of State and UTs.
The members of Rajya Sabha are elected by the elected
members of the State Legislative Assemblies in
accordance with the principle of proportional
representation. For being a member of Rajya Sabha, a
person must be not less than 30 years of age.
Presently, the actual strength of Rajya Sabha stands at 245
with 233 elected members and 12 nominated members.
The Rajya Sabha is a permanent body and is not subject to
dissolution, but one-third of its members retire every two
years. The term of its member is 6 years.
1. Powers of Rajya Sabha Resolution seeking the
removal of the Vice-President can originate only in
the Rajya Sabha. In Rajya Sabha any bill can originate,
except the money bill (including budget) which can
originate only in Lok Sabha.
2. Special Power of Rajya Sabha It can authorise the
Parliament to make a law on a subject enumerated in
the State List (Article 249). It can authorise the
Parliament to create new All India Services common for
both the Centre and States (Article 312).
Lok Sabha
Article 81 deals with the composition of the Lok Sabha.
The maximum strength of the House is 552, of which 530
members represent the states, 20 members represent the
Union Territories and 2 members to be nominated by the
President from the Anglo Indian Community. Present
strength of Lok Sabha is 545.
The number of constituencies of Lok Sabha has increased
from 401 in 1951 to 530 in 2019.
Members of the Lok Sabha are directly elected by the
people from the territorial constituencies in the states. For
being a member of Lok Sabha, a person must be not less
than 25 years of age.
Lok Sabha is not a permanent body and subject to
dissolution.

The President is authorised to dissolve Lok Sabha at any
time even before the completion of 5 years.
Note In 2019, the 17th Lok Sabha was elected and OM Birla
was elected as Lok Sabha Speaker.
Speaker of Lok Sabha (Article 93)
Speaker is the constitutional and ceremonial head of the
lok sabha. He is elected by lok sabha from amongst its
members.
He doesn’t vote on a bill in the first instance, but he can
exercise a casting vote in the case of tie.
He presides over a joint sitting of two houses of the
parliament
He certifies a Bill as money Bill and his decision is final.
Power and Function of Lok Sabha
Money Bill can only originate in Lok Sabha with the
permission of President according to Article 110. Simple
majority is needed to pass this Bill.
A no-confidence motion to remove the council of
ministers can only be introduced in Lok Sabha.
Any Bill pending in Rajya Sabha passed by Lok Sabha also
lapse unless President calls a joint sitting of the two Houses.
Any Bill pending in Rajya Sabha, not passed by Lok
Sabha doesn’t lapse.
Parliamentary Committees
Parliamentary Committees are appointed or elected by the
House or nominated by the Speaker and work under the
direction of the Speaker.

judicial system which places Supreme Court at the top
and the High Courts below it, followed by a hierarchy of
subordinate courts.
The constitutional provisions related to the Supreme
Court are contained in Part V in Article 124-147 of Indian
Constitution.
Article 214 to 231 in Part VI of the Constitution deal with
provisions related to High court; while Articles 233 to 237
in Part VI of the Constitution deal with subordinate courts.

State Executive
The constitutional provision related to the State Executive
is vested in Part VI of Constitution from Article 153-167.
The State Executive consists of the Governor, the Chief
Minister and the Council of Ministers and the Advocate
General.
Governor
The Constitution provides for an office of the Governor in
the state under Article 153.
Governor of a state shall be appointed by the President by
warrant under his hand and seal.
The Governor holds office for a period of 5 years.
All the executive action of a State Government are
formally taken in his name.
Governor has the power to nominate one member of
Anglo-Indian Community to Legislative Assembly.
He nominates one-sixth member of Legislative Council.
He cause to be laid before the state legislature, the annual
financial statement (Budget).
Appoints the Advocate General of a State and judges of
sub ordinate courts.
Chief Minister and Council of Ministers
Chief Minister is the real Executive Head of the State
Government. He is appointed by the Governor under
Article 164 of the Constitution.
Every state has a Council of Ministers headed by the
Chief Minister to aid and advise the Governor under
Article 163 of the Constitution.
Chief Minister allocates and reshuffles the portfolios
among Ministers.
Advises the Governor with regard to summoning and
proroguing the sessions of the State Legislature.

The State Legislature
Article 168-212 in Part VI of the Constitution deals with
the organisation, composition, duration officers,
procedures and  privileges of the State Legislature.
Only 7 states Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Jammu and
Kashmir, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and
Telangana are having bicameral system.
Parliament can create Legislative Council or abolish it on
the recommendation of Legislative Assembly of the State.
Legislative Assembly
Legislative Assembly or the Vidhan Sabha is the ‘lower
house’ of the State Assembly.
It consists of not more than 500 members and not less
than 60 members.
However, in case of Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim and Goa,
the minimum number is fixed at 30 and in case of
Mizoram and Nagaland, it is 40 and 46 respectively.
A person must be not less than 25 years of age for
contesting election of Legislative Assembly.
Legislative Assembly legislates law on subject contained
in the State List as well as Concurrent List.
The members are directly elected by the people for the
period of 5 years, unless the House is dissolved by the
Governor earlier.
Legislative Council
It is known as Upper House and like Rajya Sabha, it is
also permanent House as given in Article 169.
The number of members of the Legislative Council should
not exceed one-third of the total strength of the State
Assembly. Its strength should also not be less than 40
members (except Jammu and Kashmir).
The tenure of Legislative Council is 6 years with one-third
members retiring every two years.
One-third of the members are elected by local bodies, one
third by Legislative Assembly, one-twelfth by university
graduates, one-twelfth by the electorate consisting of
secondary school teachers (3 year experience) and One
sixth members are nominated by the Governor.
The Council elects a Chairman and Vice Chairman from
amongst its members.
Legislative Council can hold ordinary Bill for maximum
of 3 months and after that the bill is deemed to be passed
in its original form.
Panchayati Raj
Panchayati Raj in India was introduced on the
recommendation of Balwant Rai Mehta Committee
which advocated three tier system of Panchayati Raj at
the village, intermediate and district level.
It was first adopted by Rajasthan (Nagaur district on 2nd
October, 1959) followed by Andhra Pradesh.
73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 has inserted a
new Part IX and Schedue XI in the Constitution and
provided a constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj
institutions.
Part IX consist of Articles 243 to 243-0 and schedule 11th
contains powers, authority and responsibilities of
panchayats with 29 functional items.
The 73rd amendment Act, provides one third reservation
of total number of seats for women.
All elections related to panchayats shall be vested in the
state election commission.
In case of dissolution of panchayat, before its term, fresh
election has to be completed before the expiry of a period
of six months from the date of dissolution.
Municipalities
Muncipalities  are the institutions of ‘Urban local
Government’ in India.
There are generally three types of municipalities that is
Nagar Panchayat for transitional area (from rural to
urban), Municipal Council for smaller urban area and
Municipal Corporation for larger urban areas.
The Muncipalities  are given constitutional status by 74th
Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992 which added a
new Part IX-A  and a new schedule ‘XII’ in Constitution.
Part IX-A consits of Articles 243-(P) to 243-ZG and
schedule twelfth contains powers, authority and
responsibilities with 18 functional items.
Constitutional Bodies
Union Public Service Commission
Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) is the central
recruiting agency in India. Article 315 to 323 in Part XIV
of the Constitution has elaborate provisions regarding it.
The Chairman and other members of the UPSC are
appointed by the President and they hold office for a term
of 6 years from the date of appointment or until they attain
the age of 65 years. UPSC members can resign by
addressing their letter of resignation to the President.
The function of UPSC is to conduct exams for
appointment to services under the Union. It also advises
the President in matter relating to appointment,
promotions and transfers of civil servants.
There are three All India Services – Indian Administrative
Services (IAS); Indian Police Service (IPS) and Indian
Forest Service (IFS).
Finance Commission
Article 280 of the Constitution provides for a finance
commission which is constituted by the president every
fifth year or at such earlier time as he considers necessary.
53
General Awareness

First finance commission was constituted in 1959 under
chairmanship of KC Niyogi.
It is formed to define the financial relations between the
centre and the state.
The 14th Finance Commission was constituted on 2nd
January, 2013 under the Chairmanship of YV Reddy to
make recommendations for the period 2015-20.
The 15th Finance Commission has been constituted under
chairmanship of Dr N K Singh who will make
recommendations for the five years commencing on 1st
April, 2020.
Comptroller and Auditor General
(CAG)
Article 148-151 of the Constitution of India deals with the
office of the CAG. He holds the office for a term of 6 years
or upto the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.
He is the guardian of the public purse and controls the entire
financial system of the country at the centre and the state.
He audits the receipts and expenditure of Consolidated
Funds of the Union and the States.
Election Commission
The elections are governed by Part XV from Article
324-329. Article 324 (2) deals with the Election
Commission.
The Election Commission of India is a permanent,
independent and constitutional body to ensure free and
fair election in the country.
National Symbols of India
National Flag
Also called ‘Tiranga’, horizontal tricolour with equally
sized strips. There colours are-deep saffron, white and
green.
In the centre of National Flag is a navy blue wheel with 24
spokes known as Ashoka Chakra.
It was designed by Pingli Venkayya andwas adopted on
22nd July, 1947.
National Emblem
Lion capital of Ashoka at Sarnath was adopted as the

Devanagari Script-‘Satyameva Jayate’, a quote taken from

Lion capital.
National Anthem
‘Jana Gana Mana’ was written by Rabindranath Tagore.
It was officially adopted by Constituent Assembly as the
Indian National Anthem on 24th January, 1950.

Indian Armed Forces

republic of India. It consist of Army, Navy and Air Force.
The Indian army is placed at number 4 in overall
performance of the world following United States, Russia
and China.

most powerful navies. United States, Russia, China, Japan,
United Kingdom and France are ahead of India in the List.
Indian Air Force stands at number 4 in the list of strongest
Air Force in the world following US, Russia and Israel at
top 3 position.

Paramilitary and Reserve Forces
Indo-Tibetan Border
Police (ITBP)
It was established in 1962, after the Chinese
attack.
It was basically employed in the Northern
borders for monitoring Indo-China boundary.
National Security
Guards (NSG)
It was established in 1984 to counter the surge
of militancy in the country.
Central Industrial
Security Force
(CISF)
It was set-up in 1969 after the
recommendations of Justice B Mukherji.
Its objective is to monitor the industrial
complexes of Central Government.
Assam Rifles
It was established in 1835 and is the oldest
paramilitary force in the country.
Its main objective is to keep vigilance of
international borders in North-East and counter
insurgency operations in Arunachal Pradesh,
Manipur, Mizoram and Nagaland.
Border Security
Force (BSF)
It was established in 1965.
It keeps a vigil over the international borders
against the intrusion in the country.
Central Reserve
Police Force (CRPF)
It was set-up in 1939.
Its main objective is to assist the State/Union
Territory Police in maintenance of law and order.
Territorial Army (TA)
It was established in 1948.
It is a voluntary, part-time force (between 18
and 42 years), not of professional soldiers.
Indian Coast Guard
It was set-up in 1978.
Its objective is to protect the maritime and other
national interests in the maritime zones of India.

Brief History of Indian Sports
Post-Independence, Indian hockey team emerge as the
golden champions in various events.
In 1958, Mihir Sen became the first Indian to cross the
English Channel in fastest time 14 hrs and 45 min.
The 1950s and 1960s are considered as golden years of
Indian football team. In 1951 and 1962 Asian games,
Indian football team won gold.
In 1960, Milkha Singh known as ‘Flying Sikh’ ran
incredibly and created a new record in 400m race.
In 1983, India won the cricket world cup first time and
team was led by Kapil Dev.
Prakash Padukone became the first Indian to win the All
England Open Badminton Championship in 1980.
PT Usha claimed 4 golds and one silver at Asian Games in
1986 held at Seoul (South Korea).
Indian Men’s Kabaddi team won the gold at Beijing Asian
Games in 1990.
In 2005, Narain Karthikeyan became the first Indian to
drive in the formula one.
India won the cricket T-20 world cup in 2007 and ODI
world cup in 2011.
In 2012, Sachin Tendulkar became the first cricketer in the
world, to score 100 International centuries.
In 2018, Mary Kom won gold medal at World Women’s
Boxing Championships. It was her sixth medal in World
Boxing.
Olympics
Olympic games were started in 776 BC in olympia in the
honour of Greek God, ‘Zeus’.
The modern Olympic Games were started in Athens, the
capital of Greece on 6th April, 1896 with great efforts
made by French nobleman, Baron Pierre de Coubertin.
The Olympic Games are organised after every 4 years
with the summer and winter games alternative of 2 years.
The Olympic Flag is made up of white silk and contains
five interwined rings as the Olympic Emblem.
The five interlaced rings coloured blue, yellow, black,
green and red represent five continents. Blue for Europe,
Black for Africa, Red for Americas (North and South
America), Yellow for Asia and Green for Oceania
(Australia and New Zealand).
The official Olympic Motto is Citius, Altius, Fortius, a
Latin phrase meaning Swifter, Higher, Stronger.
2020 Summer Olympic will be held in Tokyo, Japan.
Due to Covid-19 these games are posponded. It will
be held in 2021 at Tokyo, Japan.
India in Olympics
India first sent a team to the summer Olympic Games in
1920. Indian athletes have won a total 28 medals so far.
Indian Hockey team won eleven medals in twelve
olympics between 1920 to 1980.
First Individual medal in olympics for India was won by
KD Jadhav as a bronze in 1952 Helsinki olympics in
wrestling.
In 2004, Athens olympics Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore
won silver medal in shooting.
In 2008, Beijing Olympics India won first individual gold
in shooting by Abhinav Bindra.
In 2016, Rio Olympics, PV Sindhu won silver medal in
Badminton and Sakshi Malik became first Indian woman
wrestler to win an Olympic medal (Bronze).
Winter Olympics
The first winter olympic games were held in 1924 in
Chamonix (France).
India has competed in winter olympics first time in 1964.
Winter Olympics 2018 was held in South Korea.
Paralympic Games
The Paralympic games are major international multi-sport
events. First such games were played in 1948 in Stock
Mandeville, England.
All Paralympic games are governed by the International
Paralympic Committee (IPC). 2018 winter Paralympic
games were held in South Korea.
Summer Paralympics 2020 will be held in Tokyo, Japan.
Due to Covid-19 Summer Paralympics are posponded.
It will be held in 2021 at Tokyo, Japan.
Commonwealth Games
The first Commonwealth Games were held in 1930 in
Hamilton, Canada.

Asian Games
The Asian Games, also called Asiad, are a multi-sport event
held every 4 years among athletes from all over Asia.
The games are regulated by the Olympic Council of Asia.
The first Asian games were held in 1951 in New Delhi (India).
19th Asian games of 2022 will be held at Hangzhou (China).

International Organisations
United Nation
The United Nations is a world organisation formed on
24th October, 1945.
The original membership of 51 nations has grown to
193 members. The 193rd member being the newly created
South Sudan.
The United Nations Headquarters is in New York city.
The UN also has offices in Geneva (Switzerland) and
Vienna (Austria), Nairobi (Kenya) and Hague
(Netherland)
Six official languages spoken and used in documents at
the United Nations: Arabic, Chinese, English, French,
Russian and Spanish.
The United Nations has six principal organs :
The General Assembly, The Security Council, The
Economic and Social Council, The Trusteeship Council,
The International Court of Justice, and The Secretariat.
The Security Council has primary responsibility for the

National Awards
Bharat Ratna
Bharat Ratna is India’s highest Civilian Award. It was first
awarded in 1954. The first recipients of Bharat Ratna were
C Rajgopalachari, S Radhakrishnan and CV Raman.
The actual award is designed in the shape of a peepal leaf
with Bharat Ratna inscribed in Devanagri script below the
Sun figure.
The reverse side of the decoration ‘Satyameva Jayate’ has
been written in Hindi with an inscription of state emblem.
Bharat Ratna recipients rank seventh in the Indian order of
precedence.
There is no formal provision that recipients of Bharat Ratna
should be Indian citizens. It has been awarded to
naturalised Indian citizen, Mother Teresa and to two
non-Indians, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan and Nelson
Mandela.
On 25th January, 2019 Nanaji Deshmukh (Posthumously),
Bhupen Hazarika (Posthumously) and Pranab Mukherjee
were honoured with Bharat Ratna.
Padma Awards
Padma Awards were instituted in 1954, and announced
every year on the occasion of Republic Day. The award is
given in three categories-Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan
and Padma Shri. The awards fall in line after the Bharat
Ratna.
There are three Padma Awards
Padma Vibhushan is the second highest National Award
given for exceptional and distinguished service in any field
including service rendered by government employees.
Padma Bhushan is the third highest National Award given
for distinguished service in any field.
Padma Shri is the fourth highest award given for
distinguished service in any field.
Gallantry Awards
Param Vir Chakra is the highest decoration of valour
award established in 1950. It is the most conspicuous act
of bravery or some act of valour or self-sacrifice ill the
presence of the enemy, whether on land, at sea or in the
air. The medal is made of bronze.
Mahavir Chakra is the second highest gallantry award
for acts of conspicuous gallantry in the presence of the
enemy whether on land, at sea or in the air. The medal is
made of standard silver.
Vir Chakra is awarded for acts of gallantry in the
presence of enemy, whether on land, at sea or in the air.
The medal is made of standard silver.
Ashok Chakra This is awarded for valour, courageous
action or sacrifice, away from the battlefield. It is highest
military award during peace time.
Kirti Chakra The decoration is awarded for conspicuous
gallantry. It is made of standard silver and is circular in
shape. The obverse and the reverse are exactly the same
as in Ashoka Chakra.
Shaurya Chakra The decoration is awarded for an act of
gallantry during peace time.
Dadasaheb Phalke Award
Dadasaheb Phalke is known as the Father of Indian
Cinema. The highest National Film Award instituted in
1969 Award is named after him.
Devika Rani (1969) was the first recipient of Dadasaheb
Phalke Award.
This award is given by the Ministry of Information and
Broadcasting.
Sahitya Akademi Award
This award is a literary honour in India, given by
Sahitya Akademi.
Annually, confers to the writers of the most outstanding
books published in 24 languages, including the 22 listed
in 8th Schedule of the Constitution of India along with
English and Rajasthani.
Sahitya Akademi award was instituted in 1954.
Bharatiya Jnanpith Award
It was instituted on 22nd May, 1961. It carries a cash prize
of ` 11 lakh, a citation and a bronze replica of Vagdevi
(Saraswati).
This award is given for the best literary writing by an
Indian citizen in a language listed in 8th Schedule of the
Indian Constitution.

Sports Awards
Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna
It is instituted in 1991-92 with the objective of
honouring most outstanding sportsperson to enhance
their general status.
It is the highest award bestowed to a sports person in
India. The amount of prize money is ` 750000.
The prize money has been increased to ` 25 Lakh from
previous amount.
Arjuna Award
It was instituted in 1961 by the Government of India to
recognise outstanding achievement in National Sports.
The award carries a cash prize of ` 5 lakh, a bronze
statue of Arjuna and a scroll of honour.
Arjuna Award has been enhanced to ` 15 Lakh from
` 5 Lakh.
Dronacharya Award
It was instituted in 1985 by the Government of India to
recognise excellence in sports coaching.
The award carries a cash prize of ` 5 lakh, a bronze
statue of Dronacharya, a certificate and ceremonial
dress.
Dronacharya Award has been enhanced to ` 15 lakh
from ` 5 Lakh.
Dhyanchand Award
It was instituted in 2002, carries a cash prize of
` 5 lakh, a plaque and a scroll of honour.
This honour is given to those sportspersons who have
contributed to sportspersons, and sports by their
performance and continue to contribute their promotion
for sports even after their retirement from active
sporting career.
Dhyanchand Award has been enhanced ` 10 Lakh from
` 5 Lakh.
International Awards
Nobel Prize
This award is the most prestigious award of Sweden in
the world. It was set-up in 1900 under the will of Alfred
Bernhard Nobel.
The Nobel Prizes are presented annually on 10th
December (The death anniversary of the founder).
It is given in the fields of Peace, Literature, Physics,
Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine (from 1901) and
Economics (from 1969).
Nobel prize in literature was not given in 2018.

Magsaysay, the former President of Philippines.

public service, community leadership, journalism,
literature, creative arts and international understanding.
Ramon Magsaysay Awards 2019 was given to
Ravish Kumar (India).
Man Booker Prize
It is the highest literary award of the world.
It was instituted in 1968 set-up by the Booker Company and
the British Pulishers Association along the lines of the
Pulitzer Prize of USA.

Units and Measurement
A physical quantity is a property of a material that can be
quantified by measurement. It can be expressed as the
combination of a magnitude and a unit. For e.g., F = 10 N.
Here, 10  indicates the unit of force (Newton) is ten  times
used to measure the force of 10 N.
Physical quantities are of two types, one is fundamental
quntities which are independent of other physical
quantities, second is derived quantities, which can be
drived from the fundamental quantites.
A system of units is the complete set of units for both
fundamental and derived, for the kinds of physical
quantities. The common system of units are known MKS,
CGS and FPS.
Supplementary units (a) Radian (rad) →Unit of plane
angle (b) Steradian (Sr) →Unit of solid angle.
A physical quantity having magnitude as well as direction
is called vector quantity, whereas a physical quantity
having only its magnitude, but does not have its direction
is called scalar quantity.
An object that is in flight after being thrown or projected is
called projectile. Such a projectile might be a football, a
cricket ball, a baseball etc.
Motion and Newton’s
Laws of Motion
An object is said to be in motion if it changes its position
with respect to the surroundings.
The difference between the final and the initial position of
an object is called displacement.
Displacement of the object can be positive, negative or zero.
The time rate of change of position of the object in any
direction is called speed of the object.
The time rate of change of displacement of a body is called
velocity, it is a vector quantity and its SI unit is m/s.
The time rate of change of velocity of a body is called
acceleration. The SI unit of acceleration is m/s 2.
Newton’s First Law Every body maintains its initial state
of rest or uniform motion on a straight line unless any
external force acts on it. It is also called Galileo’s law of
inertia.
For example, While jumping from a slowly moving
train/bus one must run for a short distance, in the direction
of motion.
Newton’s Second Law The second law of motion states
that the rate of change of mementum of an object is
proportional to the applied unbalanced force in the
direction of force.

and opposite reaction and both acts on two different
bodies.
For example, a swimmer pushes the water backwards
(action) with a force. The water pushes the swimmer
forward (reaction) with the same force. Hence, the

Living Organisms
Taxonomy deals with the identification, nomenclature and
classification of organisms.
Binomial System of nomenclature was proposed by
Carolus Linnaeus in 1753.
Five Kingdom system of classification was proposed by
RH Whittaker (1969). These five kingdoms are Monera,
Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Kingdom-Monera includes bacteria having prokaryotic
cells.
Kingdom-Protista contains unicellular eukaryotic like
Amoeba, Euglena etc.
Kingdom-Fungi is a group of eukaryotic, achlorophyllous
(non-photosynthetic) and heterotrophic organisms.
Kingdom-Plantae includes multicellular and
photoautotrophic organisms.
Kingdom-Animalia includes eukaryotic heterotrophic
organisms.
Viruses are connecting link between living and non-living.
They are parasitic nucleoprotein particles i.e. composed of
nuclei acid (DNA or RNA) and protein coat.

Human body is chemically composed of various elements
on the basis of mass composition or atomic composition.
The adult human body is approximately 57% water.
Maximum mass of the human body is oxygen, but most of
the atoms in the human body are of hydrogen.
Tissue is a group of similar or dissimilar cells of common
origin that perform same function.
Different types of organ systems in Human body are
Digestive, Respiratory, Circulatory Muscular, Skeletal,

Human heart is a muscular organ of mesodermal origin,
situated between the lungs of thoracic cavity. An average
adult human heart is about 12 cm. Its weight ranges from
280-340 g (average 300 g) in males and 230-280 g

Blood
Blood is a fluid connective tissue and composed of blood
corpuscles and plasma. It is slightly alkaline in nature
(pH 7.2).
Plasma It is a straw coloured, viscous fluid, slightly
alkaline and aqueous solution. It forms about 55% of the
blood.
Erythrocytes (RBCs) Red blood cells contain the
respiratory pigment called haemoglobin, which
distributes oxygen.
At the foetal stage, RBC is formed in the liver and after
birth it is formed in the bone marrow. The average
lifespan of RBC is 120 days.

immune system,  attack infectious agents and foreign
substances.

clotting (coagulation). It changes fibrinogen into fibrin.

Human Excretory System
The removal or elimination of waste product (in the form
of solid, liquid or gas) of metabolism from the body, is
called excertion.
Different animals eliminate different nitrogenous
compounds like ammonia in protozoans, sponges,
coelenterates from their body like urea in human, whale,
seal and frog, uric acid in insects and birds etc.
Human excreatory system is composed of a pair of kidney
having nephron as structural and functional unit.
The human Kidneys are the major excretory organs. They
are reddish brown bean shaped structures of 10-12 cm
length, 5-7 cm in width, 2-3 cm in thickness, with average
weight of 120-170 gms.
The fluid and dissolved waste substances excreted by the
kidneys (i.e. through nephrons or renal tubules) constitute
urine.
Human Nervous System
The Nervous System consists of central nervous system,
peripheral nervous system and autonomic nervous system.
Nervous system is fully restricted to animals and not found
in plants.
The neural system and endocrine system work together to
control and coordinate various body parts to maintain
physiology. The neural system is basically a control system
which involves highly specialised cells, called neurons.
Central Nervous System consists of brain and spinal cord.
Brain are divided in the three parts–Fore brain, Mid brain
and Hind brain.
Food and Nutrition
The main components of food are carbohydrates, fats,
proteins, minerals, vitamins and water. A diet in which
all the nutrients are in proper proportion is called a
Balanced diet.
Photosythesis is an enzyme regulated anabolic process of
manufacturing organic compounds inside the Ehlorophyll
containing cells, (i.e. chloroplasts) from carbon dioxide and
water with the help of sunlight. This process is used by
green plants to make their own food.

After analysing the previous years' exams, it has been concluded
that every year 1 passage followed by 2 to 5 questions has been
asked. In AFCAT, nature of questions consist of
– Direct questions
– Vocab based (Meaning or Synonym)
– Title based
Comprehension exercise consists a passage, upon which
questions are given in objective form and candidates are
asked to choose the correct answer. Candidates are required
to do regular practice to solve the comprehension correctly.
Points to be Kept in Mind
While Solving Questions of Reading Comprehension

India is a country of villages. Rural population still
dominates the urban population as far as the number is
considered. This is despite the fact that there is a rampant
migration of rural families to urban centres. Generally, the
gains of being a unit of the urban population are less than
the disadvantages and risks that are in-built in the urban
life. Crime, riots, etc are some of the examples of such risks
of urban life. The forces that generate conditions conducive
to crime and riots are stronger in urban communities than
in rural areas. Urban living is more anonymous living. It
often releases the individual from community restraints
more common in tradition-oriented societies. But more
freedom from constraints and controls also provides greater
freedom to deviate. And living in the more impersonalised,
formally controlled urban society means that regulatory
orders of conduct are often directed by distant bureaucrats.
The police are strangers executing these prescriptions on an
anonymous set of subjects. Minor offences in small town or
village are often handled without resort to official police
action. As disputable as such action may seem to be, it
results in fewer recorded violations of the law compared to
the big cities. Although perhaps causing some decision
difficulties for the police in small town, formal and objective
law enforcement is not always acceptable to the villagers.
Urban area with mass population, greater wealth, more
commercial  establishments and more products of our
technology also provide more frequent opportunities for
theft. Victims are impersonalised, property is insured,
consumer goods in more abundance are vividly displayed
and are more portable. The crime rate increases despite
formal moral education given in schools.

Answers

In AFCAT, Error Based Questions have been asked since last 2 years.
As far as number of questions are concerned, 4 to 8 questions are
asked every year.
In questions, Error part mainly consists of Tense, Verb, Pronoun,
Preposition, Conjunction etc.
Error detection means to detect the error or find the error in
the given sentence. In the sentences, the errors may be
related to the different parts of speech like Articles, Noun,
Pronoun, Adjective, Verb, Adverb, Preposition, Tense
Conjunction etc.
To solve these types of questions, one must have a good
knowledge of basic rules of English Grammar.
In error detection questions, candidates are required to find
out the part of the sentence which has an error. In case there
is no error in the sentence, the candidate has to mark ‘No
error’ as answer.
Articles
The demonstrative adjectives a, an and the are called
Articles. There are two kinds of articles

Indefinite article–A/An
2. Definite article–The
Uses of Indefinite Article–A/An
Article ‘A/An’ is used in following contexts
1. The article An is used before a word beginning with a
vowel sound. e.g.
(i) She is an intelligent girl.
(ii) He is an MP.
2. The article A is used before a word beginning with a
consonant sound. e.g.
(i) He is a university student. (ii) He is a European.
3. A/An is used before a singular countable noun when it
is mentioned for the first time representing no
particular person or thing.
e.g. (i) He has an axe.
(ii) She is a lawyer.
4. A/An is used before a singular countable noun which
is used as the representative of a class of things or
persons. e.g.
(i) A dog is an animal.
(ii) A peacock is a bird.
5. A/An is used in exclamations before singular
countable nouns. e.g.
(i) What an interesting movie! (ii) What a pretty girl!
Uses of Definite Article—The
Article ‘The’ is used in the following contexts
1. When we talk about a particular person or thing or
one already mentioned.
e.g. (i) Give me the book which you bought
yesterday.
(ii) The dress you want is out of stock.
2. When a singular noun represents a whole class.
e.g. (i) The lotus is a beautiful flower.
(ii) The cow is economically useful.
3. Before the first noun in ‘noun + preposition + noun’
construction. e.g.
(i) The Bharat of Ramayana is an ideal brother.
(ii) The gold of India is famous.
4. Before names of mountain ranges, groups of islands,
rivers, oceans, gulfs, deserts and forests, names of
countries.
e.g. The Alps, The Himalayas, The Hebrides, The
Ganges, The Amazon, The Nile, The Arabian Sea, The
Sahara, The Black Forest, The Netherlands etc.
(i) The Nile is the longest river in Africa.
(ii) The Sahara desert is one of the world’s least
hospitable regions.
5. Before names of religious and mythological books,
names of newspapers and magazines. e.g. The Veda,
The Ramayana, The Bible, The Hindustan Times, The
Times of India, The Statesman etc.
(i) The Ramayana is a sacred book.
(ii) The Times of India is a well known English
newspaper.
6. Before names of heavenly bodies, directions and
things unique or one of their kind.
e.g. The Earth, The Sun, The Moon, The East, The
North, The Equator etc.
(i) The Sun sets in the West.
(ii) The Earth revolves around the Sun.
But ‘The’ is not used before the words ‘Heaven, Hell, God,
Parliament’.
e.g. (i) Go to hell.
(ii) He will raise this issue in Parliament.

7. Before musical instruments. e.g.
(i) He can play the guitar.
(ii) She is fond of playing on the piano.
When musical instruments are used as countable

names of ships, aeroplanes, trains, the words denoting

9. Before parts of body.
e.g. (i)He was hit on the head.
