Omission of Articles
The articles a, an and the are omitted
1. Before names of days and months. e.g.
(i) She will go on Monday.
(ii) They are getting married in January.
2. Before names of languages. e.g.
(i) He cannot speak French.
(ii) She is learning Marathi.
3. Before names of subjects. e.g.
(i) She has no interest in mathematics.
(ii) Biology is his favourite subject.
4. Before names of diseases. e.g.
(i) AIDS is spreading like wildfire.
(ii) He died of cancer.
But ‘The’ is used before the names of a few diseases. e.g.
the measles, the plague, the mumps.
5. Before names of festivals and seasons. e.g.
(i) He will go to Canada in winter.
(ii) She celebrated Christmas with her friends.
If sentence is about the days of season and holidays,
article (the) will be used. e.g.
(i) He will go to Canada in the winter season.
(ii) She went to Delhi in the Diwali holidays.
6. Before names of sports. e.g.
(i) She plays tennis.
(ii) We like cricket.
7. Before the names of persons, villages, cities, districts,
states and countries. e.g.
(i) Anjali is a beautiful girl.
(ii) London is a big city.
8. Before names of meals. e.g.
(i) They take lunch at 2 pm.
(ii) Breakfast is ready.
‘A’ is used when there is an adjective before names of
meals. We use ‘the’ when we specify. e.g.
(i) We had a late breakfast today.
(ii) The lunch I had at the Rajmahal was nice.
9. After possessive adjectives (my, our, your, his, her,
their, its) and nouns in possessive case (Ram’s, lion’s).
e.g.
(i) This is Rahul’s car.
(ii) That is my book.
10. Before man, life, death, art, science, when these words
are used in the widest sense. e.g.
(i) Man is mortal.
(ii) Science has developed much in the past fifty years.
Noun
Noun is a word that is used as the name of a person, thing,
place, idea and quality of a person.
e.g. Akshay, Delhi, Chair, Truth, Love etc.
Kinds of Noun
There are five kinds of Noun
1. Proper Noun It is the name of some particular
person, thing or place.
e.g. India, Taj Mahal, Shiva, Yamuna etc.
2. Common Noun It is a name given to every person or
thing of the same class or kind.
e.g. Boy, girl, teacher, doctor, tree, books etc.
3. Collective Noun It is the name of a collection or a
group of persons or things treated as a whole.
e.g. Class, pack, crowd, army, team etc.
4. Material Noun It is the name of a material or
substance out of which things are made.
e.g. Iron, gold, copper, wheat, milk, water etc.
5. Abstract Noun It is the name of a quality, idea,
concept or a state.
e.g.
(i) Feeling Love, fear, anger, respect, pleasure etc.
(ii) Quality Strength, innocence, obedience, beauty etc.
(iii) State Weariness, tiredness, mercy, birth, death etc.

Classification of Nouns
1. Nouns can be classified into singular and plural. e.g.
Bus, Leaf, City
(Singular)
Buses, Leaves, Cities
(Plural)
2. Nouns can be classified into masculine, feminine,
common and neuter gender. e.g.
Tiger, Father, Time
(Masculine)
Woman, Lioness, Peace
(Feminine)
Teacher, Servant, Student
(Common)
Copy, Book, Room
(Neuter)
3. Nouns can be classified into countable and
uncountable nouns. e.g.
Tables, Chairs, Branches
(Countables)
Oxygen, Furniture, Happiness
(Uncountables)
Some Important Rules of Noun
Rule 1
Articles are not used before material nouns. e.g.
(i) Leather is used in making shoes.
(ii) Copper and mispickel are mined only in small
quantities.
Rule 2
Material nouns and abstract nouns are not used in plural
form. e.g.
(i) Care of the old is necessary.
(ii) Jewellery of gold is very costly.
Rule 3
Proper nouns are sometimes used as common nouns. e.g.
(i) Samudragupta is the Napoleon of India.
(ii) Kalidas is the Shakespeare of India.
In the above two sentences, the proper nouns Napoleon
and Shakespeare are used as common nouns.
Rule 4
Collective nouns usually take a singular verb and are
substituted by a singular pronoun. e.g.
(i) The jury has given its verdict.
(ii) The team has performed to its potential.
Rule 5
Collective nouns take a plural verb and are substituted by a
plural pronoun, when the group members do not behave as
a whole but take different directions. e.g.
(i) The jury are divided in their decision.
(ii) The Ministry are much divided in their opinion
regarding the foreign policy.
Rule 6
Collective nouns, even when they denote living beings, are
considered to be of neuter gender. e.g.
(i) India has a big army and it is divided
into three major divisions.
(ii) The class waits for its teacher quietly.
Rule 7
Units of counting, i.e. pair, dozen, score, hundred etc, when
used after numbers retain in their singular form. e.g.
(i) My friend bought two dozen eggs from the market.
(ii) I gave him two hundred rupees.
Rule 8
The following nouns are always used in plural form
G Certain articles of dress like trousers, shorts, jeans,
parts, etc. e.g.
(i) Jeans are in vogue these days.
(ii) Where are my parts ?
G Certain collective nouns (although they are singular in
form) like police, cattle, gentry, peasantry, clergy, people,
company, poultry, majority, artillery, infantry etc. e.g.
(i) Police have reached the crime scene.
(ii) Cattle are grazing in the field.
G Certain other nouns like assets, premises, alms,
proceeds, contents, refreshments, orders, repairs,
rations, statistics (collection of data), credentials etc. e.g.
(i) Court should make it mandatory for the ministers
to declare their assets.
(ii) Alms were distributed in the beggars.
Rule 9
Some nouns look like plural but always used in a singular
form like Mathematics, Statistics, Physics, Economics (All
subjects), Gymnastics, News, Innings, Series, Measles,
Rabies, Mumps, Rickets, Summons, Names of Books etc.
e.g.
(i) The news is bad.      (ii) Gymnastics is fun to watch.
Rule 10
Uncountable nouns are used in singular forms only.
Indefinite article (a, an) is not used before them. ‘Much’ is
used in place of ‘Many’ for denoting plurality. Some of the
important nouns of this category are as follows
Advice, information, hair, luggage, business, work, word
(promise), mischief, bread, scenery, abuse, vacation,
evidence, employment, alphabet, poetry, furniture,
baggage, trouble, fuel, wheat, rice, stationery etc. e.g.
(i) He gave me information.
(ii) He was punished for committing much mischief.
Rule 11
When two nouns depict a common possession, we use
apostrophe(’s) after the second noun if they are functioning
as one unit and expresses in singular form. e.g.
(i) Rahul and Shweta’s father has died.
(ii) Sheela and Rohit’s mother did not come in the
party.

Rule 12
When two or more nouns depict a common possession but
they are functioning separately, use (’s) after each noun. e.g.
(i) Rita’s and Geeta’s businesses are booming.
(ii) Ram’s and Mohan’s fathers are ill.
Pronouns
Words used in place of nouns are called pronoun. They are
used to avoid the repetition of noun in a sentence.
e.g. I saw a boy on the roof. He seemed to recognise me.
In this example, the pronoun ‘he’ is used instead of
repeating the noun ‘boy’.
Kinds of Pronoun
Following are the kinds of pronouns with their specific
rules
1. Personal Pronouns
These pronouns refer to the words which are used in place
of nouns referring to person. Personal pronouns have the
following categorisations
Some Important Rules of Personal Pronouns
Rule 1
A personal pronoun must be of the same number, gender
and person as the noun for which it stands. e.g.
(i) Alice is my sister. She lives abroad.
(Pronoun ‘she’ is used for Noun ‘Alice’)
(ii) Every man must love his country.
Rule 2
If a pronoun is used as the object of the verb or of a
preposition, it should be in the objective case. e.g.
(i) He was shouting at me.
(Not ‘I’)
(ii) He was teaching him.
Rule 3
Words such as, as good as, as well as, as soon as, as beautiful as,
as intelligent as, etc are followed by nominative case. e.g.
(i) When it comes to providing news, no one is as
good as he.
(ii) In studies, he is as good as he.
Rule 4
The second person should come before the third and the
third person come before the first. This is called 2,3,1 rule.
This case applies if all the pronouns are singular in a
sentence. e.g.
(i) You, He and I are good friends.
(Not I, you and he)
(ii) You and I will be punished.
Note If all the pronouns are in plural form, and sentence has
some confessing sense, negative sense or committing a crime
then 2, 3, 1 rule gets changed to 1, 2, 3. e.g.
(i) I, you and he will be punished for the crime.
(ii) We, You and They will go to the party.
Rule 5
When two or more singular nouns are joined by ‘or,
either-or or neither-nor’, the pronoun and the verb should
be singular. e.g.
(i) Either Raj or Amar is doing his duty.
(ii) Neither Ram nor Shyam has completed his work.
Rule 6
Whenever one singular and one plural noun are used with
either-or or neither-nor, the plural noun always comes
second. In this case, the verb and the pronoun both become
plural. e.g.
(i) Neither Amit nor his friends were present in their
house.
(ii) Either the Principal or the teachers failed in their
duty.
2. Reflexive Pronouns
Reflexive pronouns are the pronouns in which the action
done by the subject turns back upon the subject. They end
in -self in singular form or -selves in plural form.
e.g. Myself, themselves, yourself, itself, himself,
ourselves etc.
Some Important Rules of Reflexive Pronoun
Rule 1
A reflexive pronoun is used with the following
verbs-absent, avail, apply, enjoy, pride, resign, acquit,
revenge, exert, adapt, adjust etc. e.g.
(i) He resigned himself to his failure.
(ii) You should avail yourself of every chance
in life.

Rule 2

3. Demonstrative Pronouns
The pronouns that are used to point out the objects to which
they refer are called demonstrative e.g. these, that, those,
such, this etc.
Some Important Rules of Demonstrative Pronouns
Rule 1
‘This’ and ‘That’ takes a singular verb while ‘These’ and
‘Those’ takes a plural verb. e.g.
(i) That man is our principal.
(ii) These books belong to him.
Rule 2
Pronoun ‘it’ comes before the phrase or clause to which it
refers.
(i) It is true that India has won the match.
(ii) It is conform that he is wrong.
4. Indefinite Pronouns
A pronoun that does not refer to any person, amount or
thing in particular.
e.g. anything, something, anyone, everyone, one, anyone
etc.
Some Important Rules of Indefinite Pronouns
Rule 1
‘One’, if used in a sentence, always repeats itself. e.g.
(i) One must respect one’s country for one’s sake.
(ii) One must obey one’s elders.
Rule 2
‘Either’ is replaced by ‘anyone’ when we are talking about
more than two persons or things. Same case apply with
‘none’ and ‘neither’. e.g.
(i) I couldn’t contact anyone of the three.
(ii) None of his body parts is defective.
Rule 3
‘Each other’ should be used in speaking of two persons or
things, ‘one another’ used in speaking of more than two. e.g.
(i) We should love one another.
(ii) Shivani and Himani never liked each other.
5. Relative Pronouns
Relative pronouns are used to connect clause, a phrase to a
noun or pronoun.
e.g.
who, whom, that, which, whose etc.
Some Important Rules of Relative Pronouns
Rule 1
‘Whom’ and ‘Who’ are used only for persons and ‘Which’ is
used for things without life and for animals. e.g.
(i) The man who is honest is trusted.
(ii) The horse which I had bought was an Arab.
Note After words such as ‘all, any, none, only, alone, no-thing’,
pronoun ‘that’ will be used in place of ‘which’ or ‘who’.
e.g. All that glitters is not gold.
Rule 2
The relative pronoun ‘what’ is used without any
antecedent.It has the meaning-the thing or things that. e.g.
(i) I mean what I say.
(ii) What cannot be cured must be endured.
Rule 3
‘Whose’ is used to refer to persons only; ‘of which’ is used
while referring to lifeless objects. e.g.
(i) I have a friend whose father is a doctor.
(ii) I saw a watch, the dial of which was made of gold.
6. Interrogative Pronouns
The interrogative pronouns are used for making querries or
asking questions.
e.g. who, what, whose, whom etc.
Some Important Rules of Interrogative Pronouns
Rule 1
‘What’ is used in broad sense, while ‘which’ is used in the
specific sense. e.g.
(i) What are you doing these days?
(ii) Which institute have you joined for that?
Rule 2
‘Which’ is used in place of ‘who’ and ‘what’, when we are
referring to a choice between two or more than two things
or persons. e.g.
(i) Of the two brothers which is more intelligent?
(ii) Which is your mother in the crowd?
Adjective
An Adjective is a word which is used to describe a Noun or
a Pronoun. They are also called Describing Words.
e.g. a beautiful garden, dark humour, a self-made man etc.
In the above examples, adjective ‘beautiful, dark and self
made’ describe the nouns i.e. garden, humour and man
respectively.
Kinds of Adjectives
Following are the kinds of adjectives
1. Adjectives of Quality These are used to describe the
quality, condition or nature of a noun.

e.g. honest, kind, soft, sweet etc.
(i) Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam was an honest man.
(ii) This food tastes sour.
2. Adjectives of Quantity These adjectives show the
quantity or degree of a thing.
e.g. much, little, whole, some, enough, all etc.
Much, little, whole are always used for quantity. e.g.
(i) How much milk is left in the fridge?
(ii) There is little sugar left in the pot.
All, some, enough, sufficient, most are used for both
quantity and number. e.g.
(i) Mayank has enough money to start his own
business.
(ii) Employees have completed most of the tasks.
3. Adjectives of Number These are of two types
options:
Definite adjectives as Cardinals (one, two, three...)
and ordinals (first, second, last...) denote exact or
order of persons/things.
Cardinals are used after ordinals, if they both are to
be used in the same sentence. e.g.
(i) The first two lessons of the novel are interesting.
(ii) The last three questions of this chapter have to be
completed.

Indefinite adjectives as many, some, enough, few, all,
most, various, several, etc. are used to denote
number of some kind without saying precisely
what the number is. e.g.
(i) Many students have participated in school function.
(ii) All of my friends are intelligent.
4. Demonstrative Adjectives These are used to point out
nouns and pronouns. They are always used before the
words they are referring to. e.g. this, that, these, those.
(i) That house is very expensive.
(ii) These cookies are delicious.
5. Possessive Adjectives These adjectives are used to
show ownership or possession.
e.g. my, our, your, his, her, their, its etc.
(i) My dirt bike is faster than his moped.
(ii) Kids, don’t forget to drink your milk.
6. Interrogative Adjectives These adjectives are used to
ask questions.
e.g. what, whose, which etc.
(i) Whose wife is sitting in the lobby?
(ii) Which book do you want to buy?
7. Proper Adjectives Adjectives that are derived from
proper nouns are called Proper adjectives. They must
begin with a capital letter.
e.g. Indian, American, German etc.
(i) This Indian town has an interesting history.
(ii) I have many German friends.
Degrees of Adjectives
There are three degrees or levels of Adjectives namely:
Positive, Comparative and Superlative.
1. Positive Degree It is used when we talk about a
single person, place or thing.
e.g. (i)Manali is a beautiful hill station.
(ii) She bought a colourful bedsheet.
2. Comparative Degree This is used when we are
comparing two persons, place or things.
e.g. (i) Rashi is taller than Mukesh.
(ii) A couch is more comfortable than a chair.
Here, ‘taller’ and ‘more comfortable’ are the examples
of Comparative degree.
3. Superlative Degree This is used when we are
comparing more than two things.
e.g. (i) Amsterdam is the greenest city in the world.
(ii) The final is the most crucial match of the season.
Here, ‘greenest’ and ‘most crucial’ are examples of
Superlative degree.
Uses of Some Adjectives
This, That
•
‘This’ (in case of plural, ‘these’)
It refers to persons or thing(s) near the speaker.
e.g. (i) This book is very interesting.
(ii) These flowers are very beautiful.
•
‘That’ (in case of plural, ‘those’)
It is used to avoid the repetition of the preceding
noun(s). e.g.
(i) My bat is better than that of my friend.
(ii) Our soldiers are better equipped than those of
Pakistan.
•
‘That’ and ‘These’ refers to person(s) or thing(s) far from
the speaker. e.g.
(i) Get that dog out of here.
(ii) Those houses are for sale.
Some, Any
•
‘Some’ is used normally in affirmative sentences with both
countable and uncountable nouns. e.g.
(i) I shall buy some books.
(ii) They have purchased some fruits.
Here, ‘books’ is used as countable noun and ‘fruits’ is used
as uncountable noun.
•
‘Any’ is used in negative and interrogative sentences for
countable and uncountable nouns, when we refer to a
quantity of something which may/may not exist. e.g.
(i) I don’t have any pen.
(ii) Have you any novel?

Note ‘Some’ or ‘Any’ can also be used in a sentence without a
noun, if the meaning of a sentence is clear.
e.g. (i) I don’t eat any salad but Rahul ate some.
(ii) Sita took lots of photos of hill station but Geeta didn’t
take any.
Little, A little, The Little
•
‘Little’ is used for uncountable nouns. ‘Little’ means
‘hardly any’. It has a negative meaning.
e.g. He takes little interest in parental business.
(He has hardly any or no interest)
•
‘A little’ means ‘some, though not much’. It has a
positive meaning.
e.g. A little knowledge is a dangerous thing.
(Some, not full knowledge)
•
‘The little’ means ‘Not much but all there is.’ It also has a
positive meaning.
e.g. The little money she had, was also spent on
medicines.
(She had no money now)
Few, A Few, The Few
•
‘Few’ is used for countable nouns. ‘Few’ means ‘hardly
any’. It has a negative meaning.
e.g. Few people are happy.
•
‘A few’ means ‘not many’. It has a positive meaning.
e.g. He asked me a few questions.
•
‘The few’ means ‘not many but all there are.’ It also has
positive meaning.
e.g. The few books he had, all taken by the thief.
More, Less, Fewer (Comparative Determiners)
•
‘More’ is an uncountable numerical expression used
before plural and uncountable nouns to refer
comparison of quantity.
e.g. He wants to spend more time with his family.
•
‘Less’ is used before uncountable nouns refer to the
smaller quantity of something.
e.g. He has less source to expand his business.
•
‘Fewer’ is used before plural nouns (countable nouns)
refer to the number of things that is smaller as compared
to another group.
e.g. Fewer candidates cracked the IAS examination this
year.
All
•
‘All’ followed by a countable plural noun requires a
plural verb.
e.g. All the students were happy.
•
‘All’ followed by an uncountable noun requires a
singular verb.
e.g. All that glitters is not gold.
Both
‘Both’ is used to talk about two persons or things of the
same kind. It expresses that two persons or things are
intensely involved.
e.g.
(i) Both of them are equally good players.
(ii) Hold the ball in both hands.
Either, Neither
•
We use ‘either’ to refer to one or two things, peoples or
situations, when we want to say that they both are
possible and it does not matter, which one is chosen or
considered.
e.g. I don’t particularly agree with either group.
•
‘Neither’ always takes a singular countable noun and
singular verb. Neither is the negative of ‘either’.
e.g. Neither book is useful.
Each, Every
‘Each’ is used for two and more than two, while ‘every’ is
always used for more than two. ‘Each’ is used when the
number in the group is limited or definite, while ‘Every’ is
used when the number is indefinite.
e.g.(i) Each of the two girls gets a prize.
(ii) Every student has a book.
Another, Other
•
‘Another’ is used for an additional person or things of
the same type.
e.g. Please bring me another knife.
•
‘Other’ can be used with singular countable, plural
countable or uncountable nouns.
e.g. The other door is open.
Most, Several
•
‘Most’ is used before a noun as a determiner to speak in
general for countable items or peoples with plural form.
e.g. Most people enjoy a vacation in the Shimla.
Note If ‘most’ is used with uncountable objects, the singular
form should be used.
e.g. Most steel is used in construction.
•
‘Several’ refers to more than two, but not a very large
number. It is generally used with plural nouns.
e.g. Several people were against her.
Much, Many
•
‘Much’ is used before uncountable nouns and it
emphasises a large amount.
e.g. How much money have you got?
•
‘Many’ is used before countable nouns.
e.g. She has many books.

The Adverb
An Adverb is a word which modifies the meaning of a verb,
an adjective or another adverb.
(i) Neha sings melodiously.
(Modifying verb ‘sings’)
(ii) She is extremely beautiful. (Modifying adjective ‘beautiful’)
Kinds of Adverb
1. Adverbs of Time These adverbs tell us about time.
e.g. before, now, soon, today, tomorrow, shortly,
early, ago etc.
(i) He arrived late.
(ii) I will go to college tomorrow.
2. Adverbs of Place These adverbs point out towards
place.
e.g. above, around, away, below, everywhere, here,
nowhere, there, inside, outside, etc.
(i) Come here.
(ii) The thief ran away.
3. Adverbs of Manner These adverbs point out the way
or manner in which work is performed. e.g. so, badly,
fluently, carefully, fast, hard, certainly, well, etc.
(i) This book is well written.
(ii) The child cried loudly.
4. Adverbs of Frequency These adverbs denote how
often an action occurs.
e.g. once, twice, seldom, always, never, often, hardly,
rarely, etc.
(i) She often commits mistakes.
(ii) I seldom go there.
5. Adverbs of Reason These adverbs denote the reason
of any action.
e.g. consequently, therefore, hence, etc.
(i) He was late hence was not allowed to attend the
assembly.
(ii) He therefore went to hospital.
6. Adverbs of Quantity, Extent or Range These types of
adverbs show in what degree or how much or to what
extent an action was done.
e.g. very, too, enough, almost, partially, wholly, little,
etc.
(i) She is too careless.
(ii) The apples are almost ripe.
7. Adverbs of Affirmation and Negation These
adverbs are used to affirm an action or to negate it.
e.g. Yes, no, surely, certainly not, etc.
(i) Surely you are wrong.
(ii) She is certainly going through hardtime.
Some Important Rules of Adverb
Rule 1
Some words like hard, fast, deep, early, high, late, long, far,
near, etc. can be used both as Adjectives and Adverbs. e.g.
(i) I boarded the fast local.
(Here, ‘fast’ is an Adjective)
(ii) Sonali ran fast.
(Here, ‘fast’ is an Adverb)
Rule 2
The words-friendly, lively, lovely, lonely, ugly, etc. are used
as Adjectives only not as Adverbs. e.g.
(i) Her friendly behaviour pleases everyone.
(ii) Where did you find such an ugly hat.
Rule 3
‘Good’ is an Adjective and ‘well’ is an Adverb. e.g.
(i) Raman is a good soldier.
(ii) We all did well in the practical exam.
Rule 4
The Adverb ‘yet’ means that we are expecting something.
The Adverb ‘still’ means that something is going on longer
than usual. ‘Already’ means sooner than expected.
(i) Kamna still hasn’t filled her exam form.
(ii) She won’t have sent the e-mail yet.
(iii) I already did my homework.
Rule 5
We don’t use ‘much’ in a positive statement . Only ‘very
much’ is used in positive statement.
However, in negative statements both ‘much’ and
‘very much’ can be used. e.g.
(i) I like this movie very much.
(Positive Statement)
(ii) I don’t like this pen much.
(Negative Statement)
(iii) I don’t like this pen very much.
(Negative Statement)
Note Words like hardly, scarcely etc are negative in meaning.
Therefore other negative words should not be used with them
e.g. He scarcely recognised me.
Rule 6
In making favourable comments, we used Adverb ‘quite’
not ‘rather’. However, in making unfavourable comments,
we can use both ‘rather’ and ‘quite’. e.g.
(i) The seminar was rather boring.
(unfavourable)
(ii) The seminar was quite interesting.
(favourable)
Rule 7
With some adjectives ‘quite’ means ‘totally or completely’.
Those adjectives are : absurd, alone, awful, brilliant, certain,
dead, extraordinary, false, hopeless, perfect. etc. e.g.
(i) The situation is quite hopeless.
(completely hopeless)
(ii) The suggestion made by Kunal is quite absurd.
(totally absurd)

Rule 8
The Adverb ‘too’ goes before an Adjective or Adverb. e.g.
(i) Sakshi walked too slowly in the competition.
Here, ‘slowly’ is an adverb.
(ii) We arrived too late to have lunch.
Here, ‘Late’ is an adjective.
Rule 9
The adverb ‘enough’ goes after an Adjective or an Adverb.
e.g.
(i) Prakhar jumped high enough to reach the target.
(ii) She is wise enough to allow her son to go.

Rule 10
‘Too many’, ‘too much’ and ‘enough’ are used before a Noun.

Verb
Verb is a word that tells about an action or state. The verb is
the main word in a sentence. No sentence can be completed
without a verb.
e.g.
(i) Supriya painted the wall.
(ii) The house is being whitewashed.
In the above examples, ‘painted’ and ‘being whitewashed’ are
verbs.
Kinds of Verbs
There are mainly two types of verbs i.e. Main verb and
Helping verb.
Main Verb
Main verbs or action verbs are used to express an action
(sings, reads, writes, etc.) in a sentence.
e.g.
(i) The Sun shines.
(ii) The monkey jumps.
Main verbs are also of two types
1. Transitive Verbs These are the verbs which need an
object to complete the sentence. e.g.
(i) Never eat any fruit without cleaning.
(ii) She writes a letter on every Sunday.
In the above examples, the verb ‘eat’ and ‘writes’ require
an object to make the sentence complete.
2. Intransitive Verbs These are the verbs which do not
need an object to make the sentence complete.
e.g.
(i) They jumped.
(ii) The dog ran.
In the above examples, the verb ‘jumped’ and ‘ran’ do
not require an object and can alone make the sentence
complete.
Helping Verb
Helping verbs are used before the main verb to convey
additional information of possibility (may, can, could, etc.)
or time (was, is, has, etc). e.g.
(i) We are learning about the thesis.
(ii) You should complete the work by tomorrow.
In the above examples, ‘are’ and ‘should’ are used as
helping verbs and ‘learning’ and ‘complete’ are used as
main verb.
Helping verbs can be divided in Primary and Modal
Auxiliary Verbs.
1. Primary Auxiliary Verbs These verbs can be further
divided as following
Verbs ‘to be’–Is/Am/Are/Was/Were/Being
Verbs ‘to do’–Do/Does/Did/Doing/Done
Verbs ‘to have’–Has/Have/Had/Having
2. Modal Auxiliary Verbs Some common modal
auxiliaries are : May, Might, Can, Could, Will, Shall,
Should, etc.

Some Important Rules of Verbs
Rule 1
Auxiliary verbs ‘is/am/are’ are used in Present tense while
‘was/were’ are used in Past tense.
‘Am’ is used with ‘I’ only, while ‘is’ is used with other
singulars. ‘Are/Were’ are used with plurals and ‘was’ is
used with singulars in Past tense. e.g.
(i) I am to go to USA next month.
(ii) She was angry.
Rule 2
A plural noun denoting quantity or measurements of time,
money, distance and weight as a unit, takes singular verb.
e.g.
(i) Five kilograms is not a heavy weight.
(ii) Six miles is not a long distance.
In the above examples, plural nouns (kilograms, miles) takes
singular verb (is).
Rule 3
‘Each’ and ‘Every’ takes singular noun and singular verb. e.g.
(i) Each boy and girl has to attend the function.
(ii) Every man, woman and child was happy to meet with
the President.
In the above examples, ‘Each’ and ‘Every’ is followed by
singular nouns (boy, girl, man, woman, child) and singular
verb (has, was).
Rule 4
One of, Either of, Neither of, None of; always take plural
noun and singular verb.  e.g.
(i) None of those reasons is valid.
(ii) Neither of the girls is here.
Here, plural nouns (reasons, girls) takes singular verb (is) .
Rule 5
When two nouns are joined together by-besides, as well as,
and not, in addition to, like, with, together with
accompanied by, then the verb is used according to the first
noun.  e.g.
(i) Ram and not his friends was present there.
Here, Ram (singular) is the former noun, so the verb
(is) used ‘is’ in singular form.
(ii) Four questions in addition to the first question have to
be answered.
Here, ‘Four questions’ (Plural) is the former noun so the
verb ‘were’ is used in plural form.
Rule 6
Singular verb and singular noun are used with ‘another’
while plural verb and plural noun are used with ‘other’.
e.g.
(i) There is another bag in the cupboard.
(ii) There are other bags in the cupboard.
Rule 7
If a countable noun follows ‘all’ or ‘some’ in a sentence, then
the noun as well as the verb used will be in plural form. e.g.
(i) All the tigers are wild animals.
(ii) Some animals are faithful.
In the above examples, ‘All’ and ‘Some’ are followed by
plural nouns (tigers, animals) also denote plural form, so
verb ‘are’ is used in these sentences.
Note If ‘All’ or ‘Some’ is followed by uncountable noun, then
the verb used will be singular. e.g.
(i) All the money was taken away by the thief.
(ii) Some milk is needed.

Modals
A verb used to express the mood (mode) or attitude of a
speaker is called modal auxiliary or modals. e.g.
(i) You should regularly go for a morning walk.
(ii) They must attend tomorrow’s meeting.
Some common modals are may, might, can, could, will,
shall, would, should, must etc.
Uses of Modals
1. May is used
G To show or ask for permission.
e.g. (i) May I go now ?
(ii) May I borrow two books from the library ?
G For making informal request.
e.g. (i) May I have the salt please?
(ii) May I borrow your pen?
G For expressing good wishes, desire, wish
or prayer.
e.g. (i) May you live long!
(ii) May you enjoy marital happiness!
G For expressing purpose.
e.g. (i) She works hard so that she may pass.
(ii) We eat so that we may live.
2. Might is used
G For making request that expresses more politeness,
hesitation or lack of confidence of the speaker.
e.g. (i) Might I borrow your golden necklace?
(ii) Might I talk to the P.M?
G When the uncertainty did not happen but it was
possible then ‘might’ is used in perfect tense.
e.g. (i) You might have invited me to your wedding.
(ii) She might have come, if we asked her.
G In conditional sentences, when the expression is
introduced by a verb in the past tense.

e.g. (i) He may/might have left yesterday.

(It is possible he failed)
4. Can is used
G To express physical or mental ability/

e.g. (i) I can solve this puzzle.

G To take permission or giving an order
e.g. (i) Yes, you can go now.
(ii) You can take my book.
G In questions with ‘Wh’ words to denote
puzzleness/impatience/anger of the speaker
e.g. (i) What can he do?
(ii) How can she resign?
G To show the circumstantial possibility.
e.g. (i) You can ski on the hills now-a-days.
(ii) You can go there by road now.
5. Could is used
G For making a request more polite and courteous.
e.g. (i) Could you lend me your car for a day?
(ii) Could you please send me an application form?
G Use of ‘could’ refers past ability. e.g.
(i) When I was young, I could climb any tree.
(ii) When Ram was young, he could swim across this
river.
G To express general permission in the past. e.g.
(i) On Sundays, we could (were allowed to) stay up
late.
(ii) On holidays, I could use company’s car.
G In unreal conditions. e.g.
(i) If I had ten crores, I could build a temple.
(ii) If I had wings, I could fly to Himalayas.

indicating that the action did not take place. e.g.
(i) I could have revealed the secret.
(But I did not)
(ii) You could have borrowed money.
(But you did not)

G To denote warning or threat
e.g. (i) Anyone find involved shall be punished.
(ii) You shall be transferred if you don’t work properly.
G To denote compulsion
e.g. (i) You shall go to meet him tomorrow.
(ii) You shall complete her work by tomorrow.

Preposition
A preposition is a word used to link a noun, pronoun or
phrases to other words within a sentence. It denotes the
relation of the person or thing with something else.
e.g.
(i) The food is on the table.
In this sentence, ‘on’ shows the relation between the
nouns ‘table’ and ‘food’.
(ii) I am fond of chocolates.
In this sentence, ‘of’ shows the relation between the
words ‘fond’ and ‘chocolates’.
Kinds of Prepositions
Following are the kinds of preposition
1. Simple Preposition These are most commonly used
prepositions. They include ‘at, by, for, in, of, off, on,
out, through, till, to, up, with’ etc.

2. Compound Preposition These are usually formed by
prefixing a preposition to a noun, adjective or adverb.
These include ‘about, above, across, along, amidst,
among, amongst, around, before, behind, beneath,
beside, etc.
3. Phrasal/Group Preposition These are formed by
joining two or more words. These include phrases like
according to, in accordance with, in place of, agreeable
to, in addition to, in reference to, along with, in (on)
behalf of etc.

Conjunction
Conjunctions are words that are used to join words,
phrases, sentences and clauses.
e.g.
(i) Sheena and Reena are best friends.
(ii) The music was loud nevertheless it was enjoyable.
Here, conjunction joins the two words and nevetheless joins
two clauses.
Kinds of Conjunction
Conjunctions can be classified as : coordinating
conjunctions, correlative conjunctions, subordinating
conjunctions and compound conjunctions.
I. Coordinating Conjunctions
The coordinating conjunctions are used to connect words,
phrases and clauses of equal ranks. The coordinating
conjunctions include: (and, but, or, nor, for, yet, so).
And
It is used to combine two words, sentences or ideas.
e.g.
(i) I like to drink tea and coffee.
(ii) He eats cake, chocolate, pastry and chips.
But
It is used to connect to contrast ideas.
e.g.
(i) Andy likes red, but Sophie likes blue.
(ii) I am dancing, but she is singing.
Or
It is used to express a choice between two things.
e.g.
(i) You can eat it with a fork or a spoon.
(ii) You are making the diagram horizontally or
vertically.
Nor
It is used to combine two words or ideas both of which are
to be negated.
e.g.
(i) Ram is drinking neither hot chocolate nor coffee.
(ii) Kiran has not come nor has Shyam.
For
It is used as a conjunction of purpose or reason.
e.g.
(i) I cannot attend the meeting for I am unwell.
(ii) I am not willing to spend so much money on it for it
is very expensive.
Yet
It is used to express that something has not happened but
you expect it to happen.
e.g.
(i) I am not very comfortable doing it yet I will try
doing it.
(ii) Rocky terrorises the poodles next door yet adores
the German Shepherd across the street.
So
It is used as a conjunction of result or consequence.
e.g.
(i) Everyone was busy in work, so I brought all the
items myself.
(ii) All the rooms of the hotel were occupied, so I had
to shift here.
II. Correlative Conjunctions
Those conjunctions that are used in pairs to connect two
words, phrases or sentences are known as correlative
conjunctions.
Either.....or
It is used to show choice between two things.
e.g.
(i) Either Max or James has taken the pen.
(ii) I will drink either cold coffee or ice tea.
Neither.....nor
It is used to refuse both of the choices.
e.g.
(i) I will go to neither Jaipur nor Jaisalmer.
(ii) Neither they are writing nor are they allowing me to
write.
Both.....and
It is used to combine two ideas.
e.g.
(i) My brother is both smart and intelligent.
(ii) I will eat both North Indian food and Chinese food.
Whether.....or
It is used to express doubt or choice between two things.
e.g.
(i) Tell me whether you will do it or not.
(ii) Do you know whether it will be raining today or
not?
Not only......But also
It is used to express the inclusion of more than one thing.
e.g.
(i) She is not only a dancer but also singer.
(ii) We are not only composing the music for a film but
also directing a film.
III. Subordinating Conjunctions
A subordinating conjunction joins a clause to another on
which it depends for its full meaning.

Till
It is used to show the extent of time in the clause.
e.g.
(i) Wait here till I come.

It is used to show time, cause and reason in a sentence.
e.g.
(i) As I left my home, I found a purse.

Unless
It shows the negativity stated in a condition.
e.g.
(i) You will not pass unless you study.
(ii) She will not stop crying unless she meets her father.

It shows the negativity related to time in a sentence.
e.g.
(i) Do not go until I come.
(ii) They are not ready to pay until they get the house.

It shows the time related to an event in a sentence.
e.g.
(i) I know the time when she was born.
(ii) She is aware when they could harm her.
Rather than
This is used to show preferences or choices in a sentence.
e.g.
(i) She would die rather than beg.
(ii) I would live in Delhi rather than London.
Whenever
This shows the definite situation in a sentence.
e.g.
(i) Whenever I wanted to meet him, he didn’t come.

It is used to express the reason of an action.
e.g.
(i) I will eat a pizza because I am hungry.
(ii) We have to clean the house because tomorrow is

Since
This is used to show a time reference in a sentence.
e.g.
(i) I have been doing this since January.
(ii) She may pass since she had studied this subject.
Where
It shows place or position specification in a sentence.
e.g.
(i) I do not know where it is to be kept.
(ii) She may go where she wanted to.
Before
It is used to show a position, a time that states an event
finished earlier.
e.g.
(i) Get ready to go before the jury.
(ii) She had written a letter before me.

It is used to show a result or an outcome of any event.
e.g.
(i) She is reading so that she can pass.
(ii) India is planning to enter manufacturing so that

Whereas
It shows the contrast between the two clauses.
e.g.

It is used to put a stress on the given conditionals.
e.g.

It is used for the purpose of comparison.
e.g.

It is used to put positional stress in a sentence.
e.g.
(i) I shall go with you wherever you go.

It is used to join the two different clauses in the sentence.
e.g.
(i) She told me that she was a poet.
(ii) They know that you can be handy.

IV. Compound Conjunctions
Compound conjunctions are the groups of words (phrases)
that are used as conjunction.
In order that
This conjunction is used to express purpose.
e.g. we left a message with his neighbour in order that
he would know we did called.
On condition
that
It is used to express a condition which is a necessity
for another action.
e.g. He has been granted his freedom on condition that
he leaves the country.
Even if
It is used to express an action done in spite of a negative
condition or an unfavourable situation.
e.g. Even if you are tired please come.
So that
This is used to express purpose just as ‘in order that’ is
used. e.g. I will by car so that I can take more luggage.
Provided that
It is used to express a conditional statement which is
either a warning or requirement for the other action.
e.g. I will call you up provided that I have tire.
As though/As
if
‘As if’ and ‘as though’ are used to express an
imaginary situation. e.g. It looks as if it’s going to rain.
As well as
It is used to join two nouns (persons) or phrases of the
same rank just as co-ordinating conjunction ‘and’ does.
e.g. A teacher should entertain as well as teach.
As soon as
It is used to join two actions which happen one after
another. e.g. As soon as he finished his word, he went
out.
Some Important Rules of
Conjunctions
Rule 1
Scarcely/hardly is always followed by when/ before.
e.g. (i) Scarcely had he gone out of the office when he
came.
(ii) Hardly had I reached the station when the train come.
Rule 2
Lest is followed by should. Not is not used with it.
e.g. (i) Be careful lest you should fall.
(ii) He told his friend about the book lost he should
forget.
Rule 3
Although/though must always be followed by yet or comma
(,).
e.g. (i) Although he worked hard yet he failed.
(ii) Though he is poor, he is honest.
Rule 4
Both is followed by and and not by ‘else’, ‘but’ or ‘as
well as’.
e.g. (i) Both Sonu and Pawan have done their work.
(ii) The gave is suitable for both children and adults.
Rule 5
Rather and other are always followed by than.
e.g. (i) I have no other choice than to do it.
(ii) That's rather more than I expected to pay.
Rule 6
Neither ....... nor and Either ....... or are used in pairs. These
are followed by the same part of speech.
e.g.
(i) He has invited neither him nor her.
(ii) The step taken was either right or wrong.
Rule 7
Not only is followed by but also. These always join the same
parts of speech.
e.g. (i) He is going to open not only a hospital but also an
inn
(ii) Lily eats not only beans but also broccoli.
Rule 8
Whether is always followed by or.
e.g. (i) We don’t care whether you pass or fail.
(ii) I don't know whether he will recognise me or not.
Rule 9
The same is followed by relative pronoun that or as.
e.g. He is the same boy that broke the glass.
•
As is used, if the verb is not clear in the sentence.
e.g. This is the same dress as mine.
Rule 10
Because, since, as, as soon as are not followed by therefore, thus,
etc.
e.g. (i) As he came late, he was punished.
(ii) I will call you as soon as I arrive.
Tense
A tense may be defined as that form of verb which indicates
the time and the state of an action or event.
Kinds of Tense
Tense is divided in three kinds which are as follows
•
Present Tense
•
Past Tense
•
Future Tense
(i) Present Tense is used for an action that is happening
in the present.
e.g. I am doing my homework.
(ii) Past Tense refers to action happened in the past.
e.g. I completed this last week.
(iii) Future tense is used for an action that will happen in
the future.
e.g. I will go to Mumbai tomorrow.

Rule 1
Simple present tense must be used instead of the Present

With Adverbs of time (always, never, occasionally, everyday,

Present perfect tense is used to describe a complete action,

(i) Ramesh has eaten all the apples.
(Now no more available for you)

the National Anthem.

congratulated him.

Rule 8
Present continuous is used with ‘always’ for repeated
actions, usually when the frequency annoys the speaker or
it seems unreasonable to him. e.g.
(i) She is always complaining.
(ii) You are always finding faults with others.
In the given examples, Present Continuous (complaining,
finding) are used with ‘always’.
Rule 9
The Past tense in the principal clause must be followed by a
past tense in the subordinate or dependent clause.
e.g.
(i) I felt that she was a little worried.
(ii) I saw that the machine had stopped.
Note If universal truth is expressed in the subordinate clause,
its tense is not changed.
e.g. He said that the Earth revolves round the Sun.
Rule 10
Present Continuous denotes an action, which may not be going
on, at the time of speaking, but is going on in a regular process.
(i) He is writing a book.
(ii) I am not now-a-days learning English grammar.
At the time of speaking, the action is not actually going on,
but in regular process.
Rule 11
If two or more actions took place in sequence, use Simple past to
denote the actions. This is usually used with conjunction ‘before’.
e.g.
(i) She changed her dress before she went to bed.
(ii) He switched on the light before he opened the door.
Here, Simple Past (changed, switched, went, opened) are used for
both the actions that took place in sequence.
Subject-Verb Concord
Subject-verb concord or agreement simply means that the subject
of a sentence must agree with the verb of the sentence. Thus, if a
subject of the sentence is singular, its verb must also be singular
and if a subject is plural, its verb must also be plural.
e.g.
(i) Ram plays football.
Here, ‘Ram’ is the singular subject so verb (plays) used
is also in singular form.
(ii) We are swimming.
Here, the subject (we) is in the plural form, so plural
verb (are) is used.

Some Important Rules of
Subject-Verb Concord
Rule 1
The plural verb is used in the sentences that express some
imaginary wish or assumption.
e.g.
(i) I wish I were the Prime Minister.
(ii) She ordered as if she were my mother.
In the above examples, the verb ‘were’ used in both cases,
is in plural form.
Rule 2
When two or more independent singular subjects are
connected by ‘and’, the verb must be used in plural form.
e.g.
(i) He and I are well.
(ii) Deepak and Kapil are brothers.
In the given examples, Plural verb ‘are’ is used with two
singular subjects (‘He and I’, ‘Deepak and Kapil’).
Rule 3
The verb used after ‘there’ will be singular or plural depends
upon the subject it follows. If the subject is singular, use
singular verb and if it is plural, use plural verb.
e.g.
(i) There is a girl in the room.
(ii) There were several ministers in the party.
In the given example (i) The subject ‘girl’ is singular and
in the example (ii) The subject ‘ministers’ is plural and
the verb are also used according to subjects.
Rule 4
When two or more subjects are joined by ‘as well as, like,
unlike, besides, no less than, nothing but, etc’, the verb is
used according to the first subject. e.g.
(i) The Director as well as the dancers was honoured by
the public.
(ii) My mother no less than my father is strict.
In the above example, first subject of both the sentences (the
director, my mother) are singular in form, so the verb (was,
is) also used in singular form.
Rule 5
If ‘no’ is used before each of the two singular nouns in a
sentence, the verb should be used in singular form.
e.g.
(i) No boy and no girl was present in the party.
(ii) No man and no woman was swimming at the time.

In the above examples, ‘No’ is used before each noun, so
the verb used is also in singular form.
Rule 6
When two or more subjects are connected by ‘not only-but
also, neither-nor, either-or, or none-but’, the verb is used
according to the nearest subject.
e.g.
(i) One or two books are needed.
(ii) None but the leaders are responsible for this state of
affairs.
In the above examples, the nearest subject (two books, the
leaders) are plural in form, so the verb used is also in
plural form.
Rule 7
‘A number of’ is followed by plural noun and plural verb,
while ‘the number of’ is followed by plural noun but singular
verb.
e.g.
(i) A number of girls have participated in the
competition.
(ii) The number of boys in adventurous sports has
gone up.
In the example (i), plural noun (girls) is followed by
plural verb (have) but, in the example (ii), plural noun
(boys) is followed by singular verb (has).
Rule 8
When two nouns almost identical in meaning used in a
sentence, just for the sake of emphasis, we use singular verb.
e.g.
(i) The scheme and plan of my life differs from that of
yours.
(ii) The benefit and advantage from this business is
enormous.
Here, ‘scheme and plan’ and ‘benefit and advantage’ are
two identical nouns, so, the verbs used is in singular form.
Rule 9
When two nouns are not identical (similar, alike) in
meaning but part of the same idea and used as a phrase, the
verb used is also in singular form.
e.g.
(i) Bread and Butter is a healthy breakfast.
(ii) Slow and steady wins the race.
Here, ‘Bread and Butter,’ ‘Slow and Steady’ are not
identical in meaning but part of same idea, so, verbs are
used in singular form.
Rule 10
If phrase;
a number of/lots of/a lot of /plenty of/ a quarter of /part of /
per cent of / proportion of / none of / remainder of / two third
of / most of /some of / majority of / much of / many of / a good
deal of / a great deal of / heaps of, etc. is followed by a plural
countable noun, then the verb used will also be plural.
e.g.
(i) Most of the persons are dishonest.
(ii) Plenty of chairs have been purchased.
In the above examples, plural verbs (are, have) are used
with plural countable nouns (Persons, Chairs).
But if the noun followed is uncountable, the verb used will
be singular.
e.g.
(i) Most of the sugar was wet with water.
(ii) Lot of milk was sent there.
Here, in both conditions, singular verb (was) is used
with uncountable nouns (sugar, milk).
Rule 11
The relative pronouns (who, whom, which and that) are
either singular or plural depending on the words they refer
to. If the word referred is singular, verb will also be
singular, otherwise plural.
e.g.
(i) It is he who is responsible for this loss.
(ii) The book that is here is mine.
Rule 12
Following indefinite words can have singular or plural
verb. If the subject is singular, verb will also be singular, if
the subject is plural, verb will also be plural.
Such commonly used words are : all, any, enough, most,
some.
e.g.
(i) All she wants is to be happy.
(ii) Any friend of yours is a friend of mine.
Rule 13
If in a sentence; infinitive, gerund, phrase, or a clause,
functions as subject, then verb is used in singular form.
e.g.
(i) Swimming is a good exercise.
Here, ‘Swimming’ is used as gerund with singular
verb (is).
(ii) To Swim is good for you.
‘To Swim’ is used as infinitive with singular verb (is).
Rule 14
When two nouns refer to the same person or thing, the verb
used must be singular.
e.g.
(i) The poet and painter has died.
(ii) The director and producer of the film has arrived.
But if definite article ‘the’ has been used before both the
subjects and joined by ‘and’, this means the subjects are two
different persons and will take plural verb. e.g.
(i) The musician and the singer have died in a car
accident.
(ii) The poet and the writer have been awarded by the
President.

In AFCAT, 4 to 5 questions based on Sentence Completion has

Sentence completion comprises of filling up of the gaps

choices. To answer sentence completion questions correctly,
a candidate must understand the relationship among parts
of a sentence as well as know the meaning of keywords.

student should be well-versed in these areas of languages.

Points to Kept in Mind
While Solving Questions based on Sentence Completion
1. Read the incomplete sentence carefully and get a
rough idea of the theme and tone of the sentence.
2. The correct word to be filled in the given blank must
be in the context of the sentence.
3. You can also try each choice in the sentence by
eliminating those that are grammatically incorrect.
4. A good vocabulary and a sound knowledge of
grammatical rules will surely enable you to solve these
questions.

in the blanks questions.

subject: general_awareness
question:
Direct Format
In this format a word is given and out of the given four
options, a word is to be selected which is the nearest in
meaning to the given word.
e.g. Which of the given words is closest in meaning to the
word provided?
Remote
options:
Savage
Exp. (b) ‘Remote’ means located far away and ‘Distant’ also
means ‘far away in space or time’. So, the right synonym
for ‘Remote’ is ‘Distant’. Hence, option (b) is the correct
choice.

subject: general_awareness
question:
Sentence Format
In this format one word of a sentence is underlined or
capitalised and out of the given four options, a word is to be
selected which is similar in meaning to the underlined or
capitalised word.
e.g. Which of the given words has the same meaning to the
word written in capital letters?
Getting a WEAK mobile signal in remote areas is quite
common.
options:
Distant
Exp.(c) In this sentence ‘Weak’ means ‘Low mobile signal’.
While, Fluctuating (rise and fall); Falling (drop down) and
Distant (far away) have different meanings. Hence, option
(c) ‘low’ is the correct choice.

are given with their words.

Dead
options:
Deceased

dead, we have to consider its opposite meaning i.e. ‘not

option (c) is the correct choice.

In AFCAT, usually 4 to 5 questions are asked every year. Phrases
asked in Previous years’ exam were easy to moderate. Both type
of questions i.e. direct phrase and sentence based phrase are
asked in the exam.
An idiom is an expression, word or phrase that has a special
or figurative meaning. These are the group of words whose
meaning is different from the meanings of the individual
words.
e.g. ‘To pull someone leg’ is an idiom and it means ‘to trick
them by telling some one something untrue, not literally
grab one’s leg and yank it.
A phrase is a small group of words standing together as an
idiomatic expression and it is mostly derived from the verb
and other parts of speech. Phrases are a group of words
without a finite verb, especially one that forms a part of a
sentence.
e.g. ‘Fall out’ is a phrase and it means ‘quarrel’ not ‘falling
out’.
Points to be Kept in Mind
While Answering Questions based on Idioms and Phrases
1. Read the question with given choices carefully before
answering it.
2. Try to get the figurative meaning of the given idiom/phrase
rather than the meaning of individual words.
3. Use elimination method to eliminate the irrelevant or
incorrect choices. It will help to choose the correct
choice for the given idiom/phrase.
4. In sentence form questions, get the meaning of the
given idiom/phrase in the context of the sentence.

Verbal Ability in English

Questions based on Test of Vocabulary (One Word Substitution
and Spelling Test) have been frequently asked in AFCAT.
Generally, 4 to 5 questions either from One Word Substitution or
Spelling Test are asked in the exam.
A test of vocabulary is a test for knowledge (as of meaning
or use) of a selected list of words that is often used as part
of an intelligence test. Test of vocabulary are used to
determine the broadness of a person’s vocabulary.
Vocabulary questions are a common part of verbal aptitude
and ability tests. There are many different ways to ask
vocabulary questions as given below.
I. One Word Substitution
One word substitution is one of the integral parts of
vocabulary.
In one word substitution, a sentence has to be replaced with
a single word.
Points to be Kept in Mind
While Solving Questions based on one Word Substitution

subject: general_awareness
question:
A good vocabulary is required to solve the questions
of one word substitution.
2. Easy method to solve the questions of one word
substitution is root method. In this method with the
help of root words the correct choice can be selected.
e.g. Root word - Cracy meaning ‘rule’ or ‘government’.
A government by the people - Democracy
A government by the nobles - Aristocracy
3. Before selecting the correct choice, first read the
question with its given choices carefully.

II. Spelling Error
Spelling is an act of forming a meaningful word from the
letters in the correct order. Spelling error is an assessment of
a candidate’s ability to spell or write words correctly. To
answer the questions of spelling error correctly, one should
know the correct formation as well as pronunciation of the
word.
Points to be Kept in Mind
While Answering Question based on Spelling Error
1. A good vocabulary helps in solving questions related
to spelling test.
2. Correct formation as well as pronunciation of the
word will also help in solving the questions in
examination.
3. Try to learn new words from dictionary, newspaper,
magazine etc which will also help in solving
questions, from this topic.

Every year 1 Cloze passage followed by 3 to 6 questions have been
asked in AFCAT. In Cloze Test both types of words
i.e. grammar and vocab based are asked to fill the blank.
A cloze passage is a reading comprehension exercise in which
words have been omitted. It is primarily meant to test a
candidate’s grammatical knowledge and vocabulary power.
In cloze passage, usually a passage is given with some
blanks, each of which has been numbered. Below the
passage, four alternatives are suggested for each blank. The
candidate is required to choose the appropriate word for
each blank.
Points to be Kept in Mind
While Answering Questions based on Cloze Test

Read the passage and try to understand its main
theme and meaning.
2. Clarification of some facts or concepts and hints for
the blanks given in the beginning of the passage are
often provided in the last few sentences of the
passage. So, it is always better to read out the whole
passage first.
3. While considering a word for the blank, try to keep all
the possible meanings of that word in your mind.
4. The word should be chosen in the context of the whole
passage and not according to the sense of the sentence
only.
5. The answer of a blank may have some link with the
previous or next sentence.
6. Try to find out which part of speech is required to fill in
the blank.

Simplification is a process of reducing a complex arithmetic
expression to its simple form.

performed as per the following order.
V = Vinculum or Bar ‘––’
B = Brackets ‘( )’, ‘{ }’ and ‘[ ]’
O = Of
D = Division ‘÷’
M = Multiplication ‘×’
A = Addition ‘+’
S = Subtraction ‘–’
Firstly, the vinculum or bar is to be solved and following
the same order as given above to the operation of
subtraction.
It must be noted that the operation related to brackets also
has an order. The order of removing the brackets is
First →Circular or small brackets ( )
Second →Curly brackets { }
Third →Square or big brackets [ ]

LCM of two or more given numbers is the least number
which is exactly divisible by each of them.

Numerical Ability

From this chapter, questions asked in previous years’ exam were
based on finding profit/loss and CP/SP to selling of one or more
items from different types, discount or successive discounts etc.
In AFCAT, every year 2-3 questions are asked from this chapter.
The concept of profit and loss plays a very important role in
trade and business. Whenever a purchased item is sold,
then either profit is earned or loss is incurred.
G Cost Price (CP) The price at which article is purchased
or manufactured, is known as cost price.
G Selling Price (SP) The price of an article at which it is
sold, is known as selling price.
G Marked Price (MP) The price printed on the article is
known as marked price. It is also known as list price or
printed price.
G Profit If selling price of an article is more than its cost
price, then there is a profit or gain.
Profit = SP −CP
[QSP > CP]
G Loss If selling price of an article is less than its cost price,
then there is a loss.
Loss = CP −SP
[QSP < CP]
G Discount The deduction given on marked price of an
article is known as discount.
Discount = Marked Price (MP) −Selling Price (SP)

In AFCAT, 1-3 questions are asked in random year.
Questions are based on calculating the simple interest and
compound interest for different time period, difference of simple
interest and compound interest etc.
Simple Interest
The extra amount of money (apart from the money that has
been borrowed) paid by the borrower to the lender, is called
interest. The interest is calculated on the original principal
for any definite time, is called simple interest.
Principal The money borrowed or deposited for a certain
time is called principal. It is represented by P.
Amount The sum of principal and interest is called amount.
It is represented by A.
Rate of Interest The rate at which the money is lent to the
borrower is called rate of interest. It is represented by R and
specified in percentage.

Mixture
The new product obtained by mixing two or more
ingredients in a certain ratio is called mixture.
Mean Price
The cost price of a unit quantity in the mixture is called the
mean price. It will always be higher than cost price of cheaper
quantity and lower than the cost price of dearer quantity.

more ingredients at the given price must be mixed to produce

G Firstly, arrange the terms of the dividend and

term of the quotient and subtract the result from
the dividend.
G Consider the remainder (if any) as a new dividend
and proceed as before.
G Repeat this process till we obtain a remainder
which is either 0 or a polynomial of degree less
than the degree of the divisor.

and Military
Aptitude Test
Section 4


Every year 3 to 5 questions are asked from this chapter in AFCAT.
Majority of the questions are asked from Word Analogy while
sometime questions are based on Mixed Analogy.
Analogy means similarity or comparability. It is a
comparison between two things that are usually thought to
be different, but have something in common.
The questions based on analogy consist of a pair of
elements (words/letters/numbers) that have certain
relationship with each other. The candidate is required to
find an alternative or pair of elements which follows the
relationship similar to that given in the question.
There are mainly four types of questions based on analogy.
1. Word Analogy
2. Letter Analogy
3. Number Analogy
4. Mixed Analogy
Type 1 : Word Analogy
Word analogy is generally based on the knowledge of
words and their meanings.
Some common analogous relationships are as follows.
(a) Words and their Synonyms
(b) Words and their Antonyms
(c) Country and its Capital

Quantity and Unit
(e) Measurement and Instrument
(f) Worker and Tool Relationship
(g) Individual and its dwelling place etc.
Directions (Examples 1-3) In each of the following questions,
choose the related word from the given alternatives.
Ex. 1 Calm : Cool : : Abandon : ?
(a) Down
(b) Leave
(c) Attract
(d) Clear
Solution (b) As, ‘Cool’ is the synonym of ‘Calm’. Similarly,
‘Leave’ is the synonym of ‘Abandon’.
Ex. 2 Create : Destroy :: Chaos : ?
(a) Repair
(b) Harmony
(c) Anarchy
(d) Weak
Solution (b) As, ‘Destroy’ is the antonym of ‘Create’.
Similarly, ‘Harmony’ is the antonym of ‘Chaos’.
Ex. 3 Hare: Burrow :: Owl : ?
(a) Hole
(b) Hive
(c) Nest
(d) Barn
Solution (d) As, ‘Burrow’ is the dwelling place of ‘Hare’.
Similarly, ‘Barn’ is the dwelling place of ‘Owl’.
Ex. 4 Resistance is related to Ohm, in the same way
as Current is related to……… .
(a) Joule
(b) Volt
(c) Ampere
(d) Watt
Solution (c) ‘Ohm’ is the unit of ‘Resistance’. Similarly,
‘Ampere’ is the unit of ‘Current’.
Ex. 5 Blood Pressure is related to
sphygmomanometer, in the same way as wind is related
to ……… .
(a) Anemometer
(b) Odometer
(c) Hygrometer
(d) Seismograph
Solution (a) ‘Sphygmomanometer’ is used to measure the
‘Blood Pressure’. Similarly, ‘Anemometer’ is used to measure
the speed of ‘Wind’.
Ex. 6 College is related to student, in the same way as
Hospital is related to ……… .
(a) Doctor
(b) Nurse
(c) Medicine
(d) Patient
Solution (d) In the college, education is given to students, in
the same way treatment is given to patients in hospital.
Directions (Examples 7 and 8) For each of the following questions,
select the answer pair that expresses a relationship most similar to that
expressed in the given pair.
Ex. 7 Japan : Tokyo :: ?
(a) Canada : Ottawa
(b) Afghanistan : Tehran
(c) Egypt : Athens
(d) Iraq : Kabul
Solution (a) Tokyo is the capital of Japan. The same
relationship is followed by Canada : Ottawa. i.e. Ottawa is
the capital of Canada.
Ex. 8 Lotus Temple : Delhi :: ?
(a) Jama Masjid : Patna
(b) Hawa Mahal : Kolkata
(c) Char Minar : Hyderabad
(d) Amarnath Cane : Ahmedabad
Solution (c) As, ‘Lotus Temple’ is located in ‘Delhi’, in the
same way ‘Char Minar’ is located in ‘Hyderabad’.
Type 2 : Letter Analogy
In letter analogy, letters are generally moved some steps
forward or backward, reversed in whole or in sections or
have some common identity between each other.

From this chapter, 3 to 5 questions are asked in AFCAT.
Questions asked from classification are based on Words based
classification.
Classification means categorisation of something based on
its properties. The question based on classification consists
of four elements (words/letters/numbers). Out of those,
three elements have some similar properties and so form a
group. The candidate is required to find the element that
does not belong to that group.
Classification based questions can be classified into four
types.
Type 1 : Classification Based on Words
In word classification, candidate has to identify the odd
word that does not belong to the group.
Directions (Examples 1-3) In the following questions, choose
the one which is different from the others.
Ex. 1
(a) Tape Recorder
(b) TV
(c) Gramophone

Radio

Type 1 : Number Series
It comprises of numbers or digits that follow a particular
pattern. For example 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, … . There are mainly two
types of questions asked based on number series.
(i) Inserting the Missing Number
In this type of questions, a number series is given with one or
more terms missing. The candidate is required to understand
the pattern of the series and find the missing term(s).
Directions (Examples 1 and 2) Find the missing term in each
of the following series.
Ex. 1 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, ?
options:
50
Solution (a) In the given series, the difference between any
two consecutive elements is same i.e. 5.
Ex. 2 1, 3, 9, 27, 81, ?
(a) 271
(b) 243
(c) 186
(d) 291
Solution (b) In the given series, each term is multiplied
with 3 to get the next term.
(ii) Finding the Wrong Number
In this type of questions, a series is given and one of its
term is incorrect and does not fit into the series. The
candidate is required to understand the pattern of the
series and find the wrong number.
Directions (Examples 3 and 4) In the following series, only
one term is wrong. Find out the wrong term.
Ex. 3 400, 200, 100, 50, 30, 12.5
(a) 100
(b) 50
(c) 30
(d) 125
Solution (c) In the given series, each element is divided by
2 to get the next element.
Hence, 30 is the wrong number.
Ex. 4 1, 2, 4, 6, 11, 16, 22
(a) 2
(b) 4
(c) 6
(d) 16
Solution (c) In the given series, the difference between two
consecutive numbers is in increasing order, i.e. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Hence, 6 is the wrong number.
Type 2 : Alphabet Series
It consists of a series of single, pair or group of letters or
combination of letters and numbers.
It can further be classified into three types.
(i) Letter series It comprises of letters of English
alphabet that follows a particular pattern.
For example A, C, E, G, I, K, …
(ii) Alpha-numeric series It comprises of both letters and
numbers which are present in jumbled format but
follows a particular pattern.
For example A2, D4, G8, J16, M32, …
(iii) Continuous Pattern series It consists of letters of
English alphabet where a group of letters follows a
particular pattern.
For example aabaabaabaabaab …
In such type of questions, an alphabet/alpha-numeric
series is given with one or more terms missing. The
candidate is required to understand the pattern of the
series and find the missing terms.

Type 3 : Substitution Coding
In this category, a series of words is given and each word
of this series is coded with another word. The candidate is
required to answer the question in the substituted code
language.
Ex. 7 If ‘Orange’ is called ‘Butter’, ‘Butter’ is called as
‘Soap’, ‘Soap’ is called as ‘Ink’ and ‘Ink’ is called as
‘Red’, then what is used for washing clothes?
(a) Red
(b) Butter
(c) Ink
(d) Soap
Solution (c) We use ‘Soap’ to wash our clothes. But here
‘Soap’ is called as ‘Ink’. Therefore, ‘Ink’ is used for washing
the clothes.
Type 4 : Message Coding
In this category, some messages are given in coded
language. The candidate is required to find the code for a
particular word or a message based on the information
provided.
Ex. 8 In a certain code language ‘he is good’ is written
as ‘pa ka na’ and ‘ she is brave’ is written as ‘ ra ka da’, find
the code for ‘is’.
(a) ka
(b) na
(c) da
(d) ra
Solution (a)
Here ‘is’ is common in both the messages. Similarly, the code
‘ka’ is common in the codes of both the messages.
So, ‘is’ →ka.
Ex. 9 In a certain code language ‘go to school’ = 125,
‘study in school’ = 146 and ‘run to school’ = 135
Which digit is used for ‘run’?
(a) 6
(b) 2
(c) 3
(d) 1
Solution (c)
Here, ‘school’ is common in all the messages. Similarly, the
code digit ‘1’ is common in all codes.
So
school →1
Also, ‘to’ is common in 1st and 3rd message and the code
digit ‘5’ is common in 1st and 3rd message code.
So,
to →5
Now, from Eq. (iii) to →5, school →1
∴
run →3

Direction is the general position of one object with respect
to another object.
Main Directions & Cardinal Directions
There are four main directions i.e. North (N), South (S),
East (E) and West (W) and four cardinal directions
(Directions between two adjacent main directions)
i.e. North-East (N-E), South-East (S-E), South-West (S-W)
and North-West (N-W).
Angle of Movement
When a person moves in the direction of motion
of a clock, then the movement is said to be clockwise.
When a person moves in the direction opposite to the
motion of a clock, then the movement is said to be
anti-clockwise.
Shadow at the Time of Sunrise & Sunset
In the morning, Sunrises in the East and in the evening,
Sunsets in the West.

three hands, i.e. a short hand that indicates hour, a long
hand that indicates minute and a very thin long hand to
indicate second.

Calendar
A calendar is a systematic arrangement of days, weeks and
months in a defined pattern.
G The smallest unit of a calendar is a day.
G A group of 7 days is called a week.
G A month is the 12th part of the year.
G A year is the amount of time taken by Earth to make one
revolution around the Sun.
There are two types of year
(i) Ordinary year = 365 days (52 weeks + 1 day)
(ii) Leap year = 336 day (52 weeks + 2 days)
Note A year divisible by 4 is a leap year. A century
(period of 100 yr) is a leap year, when it is exactly divisible
by 400.

Syllogism is a Greek word which means inference or
deduction. It is a deductive argument in which conclusion
has to be drawn from the given statements.
In this type of questions, a set of statements alongwith two
or more conclusions is given. On the basis of these
statements, candidates are required to check the correctness
of conclusions whether the conclusion follows from the
statement or not.

In AFCAT, generally 1 question is asked from this chapter based on
one statement and two conclusions.
‘Conclusion’ means ‘a fact that can truly be inferred from
the contents of a given statement or passage’. It is an
opinion or decision that is formed after a period of thought
or research on some facts or sentence stated by someone. A
consequent effect has always to be analysed before reaching
to final result or conclusion of a given premise.
You are required to analyse the given statements,
understand their direct/indirect implications and then
decide which of the given conclusions follows logically.
Important Points to be Considered
While Reaching on a Conclusion
G To reach to a conclusion think only about the given
information. There is no need to use, assume anything else
or add any further or extra information from outside.
G If definitive words like all, always, atleast, only, exactly
and so on are used, then such words make the
conclusion invalid or ambiguous.
G If the conclusion is provided with a stated example, then
the conclusion is invalid.
G There are two types of questions based on statement and
conclusion (infrence) which are generally asked.
Type 1 : One Statement and Two Conclusions
In this type of questions, we have one statement and two
conclusions. We have to analyse which of the conclusions
support the statement.
Directions (Examples 1-3) In each of the following
questions, a statement is given followed by two conclusions
numbered I and II. Read the statement and decide which of
the conclusions follows logically.
Give Answer
(a) If only Conclusion I follows
(b) If only Conclusion II follows
(c) If both Conclusions I and II follow
(d) If neither Conclusion I nor II follows
Ex. 1. Statement These apples are too expensive to be bad.
Conclusions
I. When apples are in short supply, the prices go up.
II. The higher the selling price, the superior is the quality of
the commodity.
Solution (b) Clearly, ‘Too expensive to be bad’ means that it
cannot be bad because it is expensive it means that apples with
higher cost are good . But Conclusion I, short supply favours
rising of price is irrelevant to the statement.
Ex. 2. Statement Cases of bride burning for dowry are not
uncommon.
Conclusions
I. Inspite of anti-dowry laws, the ill practice continues.
II. The punishment inflicted on the party concerned is not
sufficient.
Solution (a) These cases are not uncommon means inspite of
anti-dowry laws, the ill practice continues.
Ex. 3. Statement Only good men die on time.
Conclusions
I. No good people live till being old.
II. Every person who live till being old is bad.
Solution (d) Both conclusions have the same meaning. Means
bad person live till they are old. But according to statement,
only good men die in time. Hence, neither Conclusion I nor II
follows.
Type 2 : More than One Statement and
Two/Three Conclusions
In this type of questions, we deal with problems, which
have more than one statements and two/three conclusions.
We have to analyse which of the conclusions supports the
statement.
Directions (Examples 4 and 5) In the following questions
two statements are given followed by two
Conclusions/inferences I and II. You have to consider the
two statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance
from commonly known facts. You have to decide which of the
given conclusions/inference, if any follow from the given
statements.
Give Answer
(a) Only Conclusion/inference I follows
(b) Only Conclusion/inference II follows
(c) Both Conclusions/inference I and II follow
(d) Either Conclusion/inference I or II follows
Ex. 4. Statements 60% of government employees went on
strike.
Mr. Gopal is a government employee.
Conclusions
I. Mr. Gopal went on strike.
II. Mr. Gopal did not participate in the strike.

Hence, either Conclusion I or II follows.
Ex. 5. Statements
Lawyers marry only fair girls.
Shobha is very fair.

I. Shobha is married to a lawyer.

Solution (d) The statement I is talking about a condition with

1-2 questions were asked from this chapter in random years.
Questions are asked based on one statement followed by two
assumptions.
Statement is an information or a fact related to any general
subject and assumption is the hidden or unsaid part of the
statement which a person assumes before stating some fact
or statement.
When we analyse assumption, we find that when one says
or writes something, he does not put everything into words
and leaves some part unsaid or unwritten. He does so
because he takes this unsaid part for granted. In other
words, he thinks this unsaid part will be understood
without saying and there is no need to put this (unsaid part)
into words.
In this type of questions, a statement is followed by two or
more assumptions. The candidate is required to assess the
given statement and decide, which of the given
assumptions is implicit in the statement.
Important Points to be Considered
While Selecting Correct Assumptions
G It should be directly related to the statement.
G It should not be ambiguous.
G It should not be superfluous.
G It should not be merely repetition of the statement.
G It should not be the argument drawn from the statement.
G It should not include words like ‘all’, ‘every’, ‘each’, ‘only’,
etc.
G It may include words related to any possibility, such as
may be, possibly, etc.
G It can be many, in numbers, based on a single statement.
Directions (Examples  1 and 2) One statement is given in
each question mentioned below, followed by two assumptions
I and II. You have to consider the statement and the
following assumptions and decide which of the assumptions
is implicit in the statement.
Give Answer

If only Assumption II is implicit
If neither Assumption I nor II is implicit

If both Assumptions I and II are implicit

In AFCAT, every year 3-4 questions are asked, from Figure Analogy.
Questions are mainly based on rotation of elements, replacement of
elements, increase/decrease in number of elements inside the figure etc.
Analogy refers to correspondence or similarity in relationship.
When a figure exhibits some kind of relationship with another
figure on some basis, then the two figures are said to be
analogous to each other.
The basis for establishing such relationship between the different
figures are given below
G Based on shape and size
G Based on orientation of figure
G Based on number of elements
G Based on inversion (vertically or horizontally)
G Rotation of figure
G Movement of figure
G Replacement of positions of elements

problem figures and answer figures are given.

3-5 questions are always asked from Figure Classification in
AFCAT exam. Questions are mainly based on number of lines or
elements, rotation, division of figures, direction of arrows etc.
Classification is the process of putting things or objects into
a group and then finding the different object or thing that
does not belong to the group.
In this chapter, we deal with questions which have a set of
four figures, out of which all, except one, are alike or have
some common nature/characteristics. You  have to select
that exclusively different figure from the given set.
Criteria for Selecting Similar-Dissimilar Figures
There are several criteria used for establishing similar
characteristics between the figures, like rotation of same
figure, division of figures, number of elements or lines,
interior-exterior consideration of elements etc.
By observing the above said relation candidate can easily
find the correct answer.
Examples given below, will give you a better idea about the type of
questions asked.

three are similar in a certain way and so form a group. Find
out the figure which does not belong to the group.

different from the others.

Solution (d) All the figures, except figure (d) are made of
straight lines. But figure (d) is not, thus, it is different.

Solution (a) All the figures except figure (a), contain the same

and three white squares.

2-3 questions are asked from this chapter in AFCAT.
Questions are based on rotation of elements either in

Series is a continuous sequence of figures following a
certain defined pattern.
A series of figures is formed when each of the
consecutive figures of the series is obtained from the
previous figure by following a certain pattern like
clockwise or anti-clockwise rotation, movement of
symbols inside the figure, addition or deletion of
designs etc.
The problems based on series consist of four/five
figures following a definite sequence forming a set of
problem figures followed by four other figures forming
a set of answer figures. You are required to select one
of the figures from the set of answer figures which will
continue the same sequence correctly.
To solve questions on series a candidate must have a clear
vision of the concept like rotation, angles, steps of movement,
different positions etc. which are discussed below
1. Rotational Direction
The rotational direction basically states the clockwise
(in the direction of motion of clock’s hands) and
anti-clockwise (opposite to the direction of motion of
clock’s hands) directions.
2. Position of Designs
The candidate should be aware of the designs and their
positions to gauge their movement. Different positions
have been marked in the given figure.
3. Angular Movement of Designs
The candidate should be aware about the angular movement
of designs in clockwise and anti-clockwise directions.
Clockwise and anti-clockwise movement of angles is shown in
the given figure.

In AFCAT, 3-5 questions are always asked from this chapter.
Questions are mainly based on completing the square pattern.
Figure completion is a process to find out the missing part
of an incomplete figure to complete it.
In this chapter, we deal with the questions in which a part,
of the figure is missing and the candidate is asked to find
the missing part from the given option figures.
To find the missing part, you are required to understand
the general structure of the figure, then choose the correct
alternative.

about the types of questions generally asked.

figure with four alternatives is given. In one of the answer
figures, the problem figure is hidden or embedded or
vice-versa.
